Kansas, like Kentucky, has had two tune-up games against Fordham and MTSU. So this will be a big step up in talent, too.

How will Tyran Stokes handle the pressure? Emotions will be high on both sides. Stokes is suiting up against the home-state team he spurned. Will Stokes let the narrative get to him, or will the top-ranked freshman rise to the occasion under the bright lights of the Champions Classic?

Can Kentucky avoid a slow start against elite competition? Kentucky has struggled with slow starts under Mark Pope in seasons prior. A team like Kansas will not let you back into the game if you surrender a 10-point lead in the first five minutes.

#2820. Op-ed: In Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged China spy scandal, there's plenty of blame to go around

To learn more about the CNBC CFO Council, visit cnbccouncils.com/cfo

In June 2013, President Barack Obama welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to Sunnylands, a secluded California estate, for an informal summit. Behind the diplomatic pleasantries, Obama confronted Xi over Chinese state-directed cyber-enabled espionage and theft of American intellectual property, warning that such activities threatened American companies and the broader bilateral relationship.

Thirteen years after the Sunnylands Summit, the threat has evolved significantly as the race to dominate AI frames the U.S.-China relationship. The stakes are higher, the technology more consequential, and the vulnerabilities increasingly involve attempts to compromise or coopt the "key man" at the helm of the nation's top technology companies.

With the unfolding scandal involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the blame should start with the CEO himself, but it should not end there. The situation illustrates a failure of Silicon Valley, corporate and political leadership at a much wider level.

Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair with a woman identified in reporting as Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. American intelligence officials reportedly believe she was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information and potentially influence Nvidia's efforts to loosen American semiconductor export restrictions. China denies the allegations.

Nvidia's independent directors have launched an investigation, and so far, they say no compromise of company secrets or national security information has been established. But the problem extends well beyond Huang or Nvidia. Focusing exclusively on whether proprietary technology or trade secrets were transferred fundamentally misunderstands the potential intelligence value of such an operation.

For Beijing, gaining insight into, influencing, or potentially compromising American technology policymaking could be equally valuable. Advance knowledge of export-control deliberations, regulatory intentions, negotiating positions, or divisions within the administration could provide strategic advantages without a single semiconductor design being stolen.

The Trump administration reportedly received warnings about the relationship before the scandal became public. Nevertheless, Huang remained an influential participant in semiconductor policy discussions while advocating greater access to China's market.

New reporting also raises questions about interactions between Nvidia and Commerce Department officials during an investigation into Megaspeed, subsequently transferred to the Justice Department. No improper influence has been established, but corporate access to government decision-making deserves scrutiny alongside proprietary technology.

Whether appropriate protective measures were taken remains unclear. President Donald Trump's public defense of Huang — saying that Huang told him he had no idea the woman could be a spy and that he trusted the CEO, and that if national intelligence had warned the president about this threat, as has been reported, he didn't remember — hardly conveyed the urgency warranted by allegations of a foreign intelligence operation targeting a strategically indispensable American company.

Trump has met Xi three times since returning to office, with two additional encounters anticipated in November and December. These meetings offer Trump an opportunity to follow Obama's example by confronting Xi directly over Chinese state-directed or sponsored espionage targeting American technology companies, their executives, and potentially the U.S. policymaking process.

It is also time for a more formal check from Congress on Silicon Valley, which has long celebrated the visionary founder, the indispensable executive whose genius supposedly transcends conventional corporate management and traditional corporate governance. Investors have rewarded this concentration of authority, while boards have all too frequently accommodated it.

Corporate governance professionals call this "Key Man" risk: excessive organizational dependence on an individual whose departure, financial misconduct, or moral compromise could materially damage the enterprise. In the artificial intelligence era, this risk becomes considerably more dangerous. When a handful of executives control technologies central to America's economic competitiveness, military capabilities, and intelligence advantages, their personal vulnerabilities become potential national security vulnerabilities.

When those executives also enjoy extraordinary access to the White House and senior policymakers, they become potential conduits for foreign intelligence collection and influence directed not simply at their companies, but at the American people and American policy itself.

Congress has opportunities to strengthen America's defenses and must act immediately.

The AI OVERWATCH Act would strengthen oversight of advanced semiconductor exports and associated national security licensing conditions.

The MATCH Act would address weaknesses in restrictions on advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment, including foreign suppliers and servicing arrangements.

The Chip Security Act would strengthen mechanisms for tracking advanced chips and detecting diversion.

Importantly, the Remote Access Security Act would extend export-control authorities to certain remote access arrangements, including cloud computing, addressing the possibility that restricted American technological capabilities could be accessed without physically exporting the underlying equipment.

Together, these measures address important technological and regulatory gaps and vulnerabilities. But controlling chips, equipment, and computing access admittedly will not solve the human vulnerabilities problem — the so-called "Key Man" risks to U.S. technology supremacy and national security.

Most of these bills have a good amount of Congressional bipartisan support. However, they have encountered stiff resistance from the technology industry and their lobbyists, and some very detailed disagreements over specifics of export-control policy. There has also been uncertainty about White House support for these bills and an unwillingness by the Republican-controlled Congress to get on the wrong side of the White House. However, there is no doubt in my mind the Nvidia controversy has given supporters a new argument for action. The Democratic takeover of both chambers could further strengthen congressional oversight and an appetite for codifying much of this into law using these pieces of legislation.

There should also be a serious discussion among key U.S. government and corporate governance experts about whether strategically important technology companies need explicit board-level counterintelligence responsibilities, independent executive-security assessments, and confidential mechanisms for reporting foreign intelligence approaches to the appropriate channels.

This is not about morally policing executives' private lives. It is about recognizing that individuals controlling America's most sensitive technologies, and influencing the policies governing them, are valuable intelligence targets and assets if compromised.

Unfortunately, the Trump administration's broader philosophy appears to emphasize voluntary industry commitments and confidence in technology executives' ability to police themselves. Morality is not a governance system. Personal assurances are not counterintelligence safeguards. Importantly, shareholder interests are not always synonymous with the national interest.

Obama understood at Sunnylands that protecting American innovation required confronting China directly. That engagement helped to clearly articulate American redlines against cyber-enabled theft of intellectual property for commercial advantage.

Trump now has an opportunity, and a responsibility, to extend that principle to today's intelligence threats. At his forthcoming meetings with Xi, he should make clear that state-directed or sponsored operations targeting American technology executives and attempts to compromise U.S. technology policymaking are unacceptable and carry consequences for the bilateral relationship.

But confronting Beijing is only half the responsibility. Washington must also confront weaknesses within the body of laws governing technology access and must weigh in on America's corporate institutions and governance.

America cannot declare artificial intelligence essential to national security while leaving protection of its technology, executives, and policymaking process primarily to corporate discretion. The greatest vulnerability in Silicon Valley may not be the technology we export, but the people and governance systems entrusted to protect it, and the policies determining who gets access to it.

Neither Congress nor the White House should be comfortable leaving that responsibility to Silicon Valley's own moral code.

—By Dewardric McNeal, Managing Director and Senior Policy Analyst at Longview Global, and a CNBC Contributor. He worked in the U.S. Department of Defense as an East Asia and China security relations expert during the Obama administration.

#2819. The AI ‘credit card’ is getting costlier as CoreWeave bond yield tops 16%

Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit.

That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away."

That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave. The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155.

"We've had plenty of warnings from the credit space," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, "so we'll have to see if credit goes any further."

Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including Nvidia, Broadcom, and Amazon.com.

CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom's CDS is up 49%, while Amazon's has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia's spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for Oracle and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk.

Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line.

The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity.

Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she's not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the state legislature passes protections for communities.

None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield.

The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins.

The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments.

Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow.

"Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank.

Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028.

As for the risk? "Downside to these forecasts exists from a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure projects on the back of the Blue Wave, which will reduce capex needs and thus debt market funding," BofA said in a note.

-CNBC's Nick Wells and Michael Bloom contributed reporting

#2818. Kirk Cousins-Fernando Mendoza leads Las Vegas Raiders’ talk in Week 10 NFL Power Rankings

In a surprise twist, the Las Vegas Raiders traded quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings shortly before the NFL trade deadline pass on Tuesday afternoon, despite still being alive in the AFC playoff picture with a chance at earning the third and final Wild Card spot. Coincidentally, the primary focus surrounding the Raiders in the Week 10 NFL Power Rankings was when it's time to turn the reins over to Fernando Mendoza.

We have our answer now, but let's dive into what a few in the media were thinking before the deal took place.

Sunday's result wasn't a low point, but it was a sign we're nearing the transition of quarterback power from Kirk Cousins to Fernando Mendoza. Frankly, the Raiders are still operating on the positive side of matters, playing generally competitive football that is, at minimum, entertaining in most weeks. The defense is disintegrating, though, which doesn't bode well for their outlook. — Nick Shook

Well, the transition is official, and Mendoza's first start comes this weekend against a very good Seattle Seahawks defense. That's a tough assignment for a quarterback's first NFL start, but the matchup could tilt in Las Vegas' favor since Seattle is struggling to run the ball and will be playing backup quarterback Drew Lock on Sunday.

Most important game of the second half: Week 12 at the Browns

This will be the Raiders' last game before their bye week. It could also determine how they handle their quarterback situation for the rest of the year. If the Raiders get at least five or six wins before their weeklong break, and Kirk Cousins keeps playing solid football, they could stick with the veteran signal-caller to capitalize on their playoff window. However, if the Raiders lose to the Browns, they could start Fernando Mendoza for the final five games to evaluate the No. 1 pick. — Ryan McFadden

This becomes a moot point after the trade. In fairness to McFadden, the Week 12 game right before the bye easily could have been the swing moment for Klint Kubiak and the rest of the coaching staff when it comes to Mendoza's first start. The Raiders' schedule softens up after the down week, and they easily could have been out of contention by then.

The Las Vegas Raiders are pretty much what everyone expected them to be during the offseason. They have a few nice pieces and a competent bridge quarterback in Kirk Cousins, but they're not yet ready to hang with the league's true contenders.

Things felt different during Las Vegas' 3-0 start to the season and even after a close loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. However, the Raiders are still clearly a year away from having realistic aspirations of a deep playoff run. The question right now is if Las Vegas has enough pieces in place to properly support rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza when or if they decide to turn the offense over to him. — Kristopher Knox

This Sunday and the rest of the season, we'll find out for sure if the offense has enough pieces to support the rookie quarterback. Having one of the most dynamic offensive weapons in football, Brock Bowers, certainly helps. Also, Mendoza might be able to unlock Tre Tucker, who had a few good games with Cousins slinging the rock.

The offensive line is the biggest question mark, as the run game has been an issue all season and the unit ranks 30th in pass-block win rate, according to Sumer Sports. However, ESPN's pass-block win rate only counts when linemen lose within 2.5 seconds after the snap (Sumer's doesn't factor in how long it takes a lineman to lose), and the Raiders are second in ESPN's ranking. In other words, a quarterback who gets the ball out quickly wouldn't be under pressure much behind Vegas' line.

A video with MMQB Podcast teammate Albert Breer from Monday's show where we argue the merits of Minnesota giving up a first-round pick to Las Vegas for Kirk Cousins. Really? Yes, really. — Conor Orr

It wasn't a first-round pick; it was a third-rounder. So, it feels like general manager John Spytek might have left some meat on the bone, but getting a Top 100 selection for a player whose days in Vegas were numbered is a decent return. Plus, Minnesota takes on Cousins' $10 million cap hit for next season, clearing the books a bit for the Raiders.

On the one hand, the Raiders, a team with low expectations, got off to a shocking 3-0 start to the season. On the other, they've now lost five of their last six games, with their lone win coming against the Jets. They've been competitive with Kirk Cousins at the helm, but it feels like reality is starting to creep in. — Chad Graff, Josh Kendall

This is interesting because the introduction mentions that the expectations each team had entering the season determined the grade. As Graff/Kendall mention, the Raiders entered with low expectations. But owning a 4-5 record when the line for their win total for the entire campaign was 5.5 is just meeting preseason expectations. Huh?

That doesn't make much sense, and I'd be interested to see what their preseason game-by-game prediction was for the Silver and Black. For most people, the Miami Dolphins were widely considered the only "gimme" game in the first half of the schedule. Many had Vegas losing to the Los Angeles Chargers and New Orleans Saints. You can probably throw the New York Jets in there too, with how many offseason additions the Jets made.

Republican lawmakers on Tuesday picked Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio and Sen. John Thune of South Dakota to serve as their respective House and Senate minority leaders in the next Congress.

"We have important work ahead of us, and I look forward to serving alongside my colleagues on behalf of the American people," he said.

#2814. Mississippi Senate: Scott Colom extends tight lead over Hyde-Smith as ballot deadlines hit

Democratic nominee Scott Colom added slightly to his narrow lead over incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate election as two key ballot deadlines hit Tuesday.

Colom, a local district attorney, as of 4:30 p.m. ET, was ahead of Hyde-Smith by 2,607 votes, out of 953,547 votes counted, with an estimated 97% of the votes in, according to the Associated Press. That's a margin of just 0.27 percentage points.

Independent candidate Ty Pinkins had 20,034 votes.

Tuesday is the deadline for resolving affidavit or provisional ballots, which are cast by voters whose eligibility is disputed or unclear on Election Day. It is also the deadline for the receipt of mail-in absentee ballots that are postmarked by Election Day, Nov. 3.

Mississippi is one of just two states whose Senate election has not been called. Alaska is the other.

Democrats so far have flipped seven Senate seats held by Republicans going into the election. That gives Democrats a new majority in the Senate of at least 54 seats in the 100-member chamber come January.

Alaska before Election Day was viewed as possibly key to the question of whether Republicans would retain their narrow majority in the Senate.

Mississippi, which has not elected a Democratic senator since the segregationist John Stennis in 1982, was on few political analysts' radar as a possible pickup for Democrats. If Colom wins his race, he would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since the post-Civil War Reconstruction Era.

In Alaska, Democratic nominee Mary Peltola is ahead by just 2,517 votes over incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, with 218,641 total votes counted, a margin of 1.1 percentage points.

Peltola has 48.6% of the total vote. If neither she nor Sullivan gets more than 50% of the total vote, the race will go to a ranked-choice round, in which the two other candidates, Gerald Heikes and another candidate named Dan Sullivan, will be eliminated, and the second choices of voters who made them their first choice will be allocated between Peltola and the incumbent.

#2813. What Kirk Cousins trade means to Raiders

The Las Vegas Raiders traded quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a 3rd round pick Tuesday. it opens the door for the Raiders play No. 1 overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza.

Here is a look at the key aspects of the decision:

Some people may have thought the Raiders could have gotten more than the Vikings' second third-round pick for a player who could potentially help them get to the Super Bowl and a player they were desperate to get. In the big picture, this is a nice get for the Raiders. They paid Cousins just $650,000 this season. They got four wins, a mentor to Mendoza and a third-round pick. Not bad.

The Raiders wouldn't have traded Cousins unless they were confident Mendoza was ready to play. Coach Klint Kubiak constantly talked about a plan and they weren't going to rush Mendoza. Again, they weren't blown away with an offer they couldn't refuse. If they didn't feel the kid is ready, they would have said no to a pick in the No. 80-90 range. Reportedly, the Raiders have been pleased by how good Mendoza has looked in practice reps recently.

I'd expect Kubiak to say this week that he thinks the Raiders, who are 4-5 and and who have lost five of their past six games after starting 3-0, can still make the playoffs. There was a report Tuesday that the Raiders were hesitant to deal Cousins because they felt like they are still in the mix. But there's eight games to go and they can make a move.

The Raiders will have plenty of holes to fill on the roster next offseason, so adding another top 100 pick is big. They should have four now. They can use it to acquire more picks. So, this is a valuable piece.

Mendoza will face the vaunted Seattle defense in his starting debut. And the challenging defense parade will not end soon. Mendoza is being thrown to the wolves, but, clearly the Raiders believe it won't be too big for him to handle.

Mendoza is in line to get just eight starts, but, according to our friends at FanDuel Sportsbook, he is the betting favorite at +350. It helps that no other offensive rookie is running away with the award.

Cousins' finale as a Raider was forgettable with three interception, but he produced and was among the league leaders in several categories. He was a tough, good Raider and helped develop Mendoza. the Raider Nation should forever have fond feelings about Cousins. Raise an In & Out double double in his honor.

Many people thought Aidan O'Connell could be traded, but, instead the 2023 fourth-round pick is a back up again after being the No. 3 quarterback this season. It won't be a surprise if the Raiders sign a quarterback to the practice squad to fill out the quarterback room. Also, expect Las Vegas to look to find a veteran backup for Mendoza in the offseason.

#2811. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2810. CoreWeave beats on revenue and lifts guidance, easing AI slowdown concerns

CoreWeave reported better-than-expected quarterly revenue and lifted its 2026 guidance on Tuesday, showing that demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure remains strong despite concerns of a market slowdown. The stock advanced in extended trading.

The earnings announcement lands at a particularly volatile moment for CoreWeave and its neocloud peers, as the market sours on the AI trade and as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the central figure in the global buildout, faces a scandal tied to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:

CoreWeave's revenue soared 168% from about $1.36 billion a year earlier, according to a statement. The company recorded a net loss of $709 million, or $1.27 per share, compared to a net loss of $110 million a year earlier. Adjusted earnings exclude stock-based compensation.

Executives pushed up their forecast for 2026. They now see $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion in adjusted operating income on $13 billion to $13.3 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha were looking for $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income, and analysts polled by LSEG had expected $12.86 billion in 2026 revenue.

In August, CoreWeave's 2026 guidance included $960 million to $1.15 billion in adjusted operating income and $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion in revenue.

CoreWeave has lost over 40% of its value in the past month, as investors rotate out of companies most closely tied to AI infrastructure. Rising interest rates have pushed lenders out of the market, raising concerns about ongoing access to capital. Some CoreWeave bond yields recently topped 16%.

"The business can execute well and still face a tougher financing environment," Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, wrote in an email. "Strong demand is encouraging; the cost and availability of capital remain critical."

CoreWeave will get most the capital it needs for 2027 through clients pre-payments and financing from hardware partners, and the company will raise "a limited amount" as well, CEO Mike Intrator told analysts on a conference call.

The company plans to raise new debt tied to a set of contracts in the weeks to come, said Nitin Agrawal, its finance chief.

"At current yields, we do not intend to issue additional parent-level unsecured debt through 2027," he said. "By contrast, the asset-level secured debt market has remained stable, with our loans continuing to trade around par value." In all, he said he projects under $5 billion in parent-level debt financing through 2027.

Fellow neocloud Nebius, whose stock is down by a similar amount, is scheduled to report earnings on Thursday. Nebius shares got a small boost from CoreWeave's results.

Both companies and several other providers of cloud-based graphics processing units are particularly reliant on Nvidia, which provides GPUs as well as necessary capital to the whole ecosystem. Nvidia shares have dropped nearly 10% to start the week as the Huang affair raises pressure on the company in Washington, D.C. Nvidia's board said on Tuesday that it hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate Huang and determine whether national security or company secrets were compromised.

CoreWeave investors are also looking toward next week, when key customer Anthropic is scheduled to debut on the Nasdaq. In its updated IPO prospectus on Tuesday, Anthropic indicated that it could be valued at around $1.4 trillion after its share sale. Anthropic has signed deals for the construction of entire data centers that will meet its needs. "We see that we're going to have long-term relationships with the AI labs," said Intrator, a CoreWeave co-founder.

During the quarter, CoreWeave said it would establish its first data centers in Asia and announced the Forge service for running and evaluating AI models.

Management still anticipates 1.85 gigawatts in active power by the end of 2026. CoreWeave is targeting $37 billion to $39 billion in full-year capital expenditures, which would imply 155% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by Visible Alpha were looking for $37.69 billion.

CoreWeave owed almost $47 billion in debt at the end of the third quarter, according to the statement. Like its bigger cloud rivals such as Amazon and Oracle, CoreWeave is rushing to bolster computing capacity for clients. But last week, voters in the U.S., where CoreWeave derives most of its revenue, rejected dozens of initiatives on data center development.

"If data center construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute becomes scarcer, and the knock-on effect is that GPU pricing may stay higher for longer," Intrator said.

He said the company does not expect risks to deliveries in 2027 based on construction at permitted locations.

"We could sell all of the capacity that we have to current buyers that are in the queue. We are choosing not to," Intrator said. We're choosing to be patient. We're choosing to bring the infrastructure to market when it is further along, because we believe that that will result in better economic output for the outstanding infrastructure that we have."

Meanwhile, demand remains robust, with the company now sitting on a $132.5 billion revenue backlog, up from $104 billion as of June.

"Should we choose to focus only on our committed backlog, we would expect capex for 2027 to remain in line with our 2026 capex investment, while revenue and EBITDA grow significantly," Agrawal said.

#2809. Millions of dollars poured into prediction markets on election night, trading on Democratic control of Congress and Texas governor's race

More than 87% of all election markets across Kalshi and Polymarket gave the right candidate at least a 90% chance of winning their race 24 hours before election night, a CNBC analysis found.

Election night showed how traders reacted to real-time midterm results, as trading activity surged and market prices shifted to Democrats after results from Indiana began rolling in before 7 p.m. on Nov. 3. Many midterm races were uncompetitive, which boosted the overall hit rate on prediction markets.

"I'd say prediction markets did pretty well," said Koleman Strumpf, a professor of economics at Wake Forest University. "But they didn't outperform the best," he added, referring to traditional forecast polls that tracked results that night.

Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.

Prediction markets saw big trades on election night.

After 8 p.m. on Nov. 3, at least $1 million was traded on a Kalshi market that incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott would be reelected. Abbott eventually lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa by more than 700,000 votes, according to the Associated Press. A little after 11 p.m. on election night, more than $1.4 million was traded on Kalshi that Republicans would not secure control of the House of Representatives.

Following the midterms, both Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan and Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour were on the social media platform X crediting prediction markets for correctly predicting races. Nate Silver, a political forecaster and founder of the Silver Bulletin newsletter, disputed the claim, arguing forecast models influenced prediction market movement. Silver joined Polymarket as an advisor in 2024.

"Prediction market probabilities strongly converged toward [our models] in individual Senate and gubernatorial races," Silver wrote on Silver Bulletin. "I was tracking this stuff closely, precisely because I envisioned that we might wind up in this sort of debate where prediction markets are low-key stealing valor from the models."

Prediction market volume on midterm election-related contracts across Kalshi and Polymarket more than tripled from the last week of October into the midterms week, according to a CNBC analysis of data published on Prediction.com. The data did not include combo markets, which bundle multiple contracts and pay out only if every leg resolves in the trader's favor.

Still, volume on midterm contracts pales in comparison with sports volume, which remains larger than all other categories.

Kalshi exceeded $3 billion in total midterm contract volume, according to the platform's website, which also includes volume for contracts on mayoral races. Last week, Polymarket's two exchanges reported nearly $700 million in volume for midterm contracts.

While prediction markets broadly anticipated Democratic control of Congress, the blue tsunami is expected to bite the industry in other ways.

Three days after the midterms, Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif, criticized the federal regulator responsible for the platforms, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, for allowing sports contracts.

"Sports prediction markets are sports bets. By effectively requiring prediction markets to offer contracts in all 50 states, even on Tribal lands, the CFTC is once again violating state law and Tribal sovereignty," Schiff wrote on X.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

#2808. Brad Holmes Makes Mike Valenti Want to Quit

The NFL trade deadline has officially passed, and Detroit Lions general manager Brad Holmes once again elected not to make a major splash. The Lions' only move was acquiring veteran safety Andre Cisco from the New York Jets in exchange for what ultimately became a 2029 sixth-round draft pick.

As you might expect, plenty of Lions fans are furious that Holmes didn't make a bigger move to help propel Detroit toward its first Super Bowl championship. But one of Detroit's most outspoken sports radio personalities, Mike Valenti of 97.1 The Ticket, apparently isn't even angry anymore.

He's just about ready to throw in the towel.

Detroit Lions general manager Brad Holmes watches warmup ahead of the game between Detroit Lions and Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Credit: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Following Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET NFL trade deadline, Valenti expressed his frustration with Holmes' approach to improving the Lions. And for someone who has made a living getting fired up about Detroit sports, Valenti sounded surprisingly defeated.

"I'm being very sincere," Valenti said on the air. "I can't. Brad Holmes makes me want to quit. Brad Holmes just makes me want to quit! I can't even get mad. I just don't care."

The Lions had already acquired veteran safety Andre Cisco on Monday, and Dan Campbell previously indicated that Holmes was still exploring his options. But as the deadline passed, Detroit elected to stand pat while several other contenders made significant moves.

When asked about Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen and linebacker Zack Baun not being traded, Valenti delivered an analogy that probably resonates with quite a few frustrated Lions fans. In Valenti's opinion, Holmes could have landed either player if he had been willing to make a legitimate offer.

"Brad's the guy who makes an offer on a house and offers 200 grand less, and the realtors like, 'I'm so sorry, but legally I have to present you with this offer,'" Valenti said. "If you go to Philly with a real offer, yes, I think you could have gotten those players."

That's an all-time Valenti analogy right there. Of course, there is no confirmed evidence that Holmes submitted lowball offers for either Woolen or Baun, or that Philadelphia was willing to trade them.

Here's the thing: Holmes deserves an enormous amount of credit for building the Lions into a legitimate Super Bowl contender. Detroit is 6-2, has won four consecutive games, and possesses one of the most talented rosters in the NFL.

But the frustration from Valenti and a significant portion of the fan base is understandable. With the Minnesota Vikings acquiring Kirk Cousins and the Chicago Bears already adding Jeffery Simmons, Detroit's division rivals aren't exactly sitting around waiting for their championship windows to open.

Holmes is betting that the roster he has assembled is good enough to win a Super Bowl without another major addition. If the Lions finally bring home the Lombardi Trophy, nobody will care what happened at the trade deadline.

But if Detroit falls short again, something tells me we haven't heard the last from Mike Valenti.

#2807. Malik Willis injury update as Dolphins QB lands on IR with groin issue

The Miami Dolphins have lost their starting quarterback, Malik Willis, for the long-term due to injury.

The Dolphins are placing Willis on injured reserve (IR), the team announced, as the 27-year-old is dealing with a groin injury.

Willis will have to miss at least four games because of his injury. As a result, he won't be eligible to return until the Dolphins' Week 14 game against the Chicago Bears at the earliest.

Willis started each of the Dolphins' first eight games of the 2026 NFL season. He posted just a 1-7 record while completing 58.2% of his passes for 1,396 yards, six touchdowns and six interceptions while adding 232 yards and three touchdowns on the ground.

That said, Willis had started to make some strides over his three most recent starts, completing 61.5% of his passes for 547 yards while logging five total touchdowns compared to just two interceptions. Now, his progress will be stalled as a different young quarterback will be given a chance to stake his claim to Miami's starting job.

Willis was revealed to be dealing with groin tightness during the Dolphins' Week 9 game against the Detroit Lions.

Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley acknowledged that it impacted Willis' play, and particularly his ability to run at full speed.

"It was tight today and you could see it," Hafley said of Willis' groin during a postgame news conference on Sunday, Nov. 8. "You could see he really couldn't open up. There was a couple of plays where I give him credit. He pulled it, he ran and he got us yards and he got out of trouble against a good defensive line. But you could see he just wasn't quite able to go full speed. So, we'll see how he's at tomorrow and we'll go from there."

Hafley did not provide much of an update about Willis' status during another media availability on Monday, Nov. 9, saying he hadn't yet spoken to medical staff by the time he met with reporters.

Nonetheless, the Dolphins opted to place Willis on IR on Tuesday, Nov. 10, sidelining him for at least four games. As a result, Miami will turn to its backup quarterback ahead of its Week 10 game against the Indianapolis Colts.

Kyle McCord is currently entrenched as Miami's backup quarterback. The 24-year-old joined the Dolphins on eve of the 2026 NFL season after being acquired via trade from the Green Bay Packers.

McCord was originally selected in the sixth round of the 2025 NFL Draft by the Philadelphia Eagles. He played collegiately at Ohio State and Syracuse, with his stint with the Orange helping to establish himself as a Day 3 prospect.

McCord has never played an NFL snap but he has played extensively across the 2025 and 2026 NFL preseasons. In that action, he completed 55.5% of his passes for 637 yards, five touchdowns and two interceptions while playing for the Eagles and the Packers.

The Dolphins will be hoping McCord can justify the faith the team put in him when it traded away Quinn Ewers ahead of the 2026 NFL season and brought in McCord in a separate deal.

Cook is presently on the Dolphins' practice squad, but he could be signed to the 53-man roster with Willis out of action.

Cook spent his rookie season with the New York Jets after going undrafted and made four starts. He failed to win any of them while completing 57.5% of his passes for 739 yards, two touchdowns and seven interceptions.

It isn't clear whether the Dolphins will add a third quarterback to their organization with Willis sidelined for at least four weeks. If Miami does, it could target either Mark Gronowski or Cam Miller, who each spent part of the 2026 NFL offseason on the team's 90-man roster.

#2806. House begins voting on Hegseth impeachment measure

The House of Representatives began voting Tuesday afternoon on a key procedural measure that could lead to the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The vote comes a week after Democrats trounced Republicans in the first congressional election since the war with Iran started in late February.

Hegseth faces eight articles of impeachment filed by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., on Monday.

Massie accuses Hegseth of waging war in contravention of Congress, carrying out extrajudicial killings tied to boat strikes in the Caribbean against purported drug smugglers and suppressing free speech by targeting Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a military veteran.

Massie is a libertarian who lost his Republican primary in May after clashing with President Donald Trump.

Hegseth, at a press conference at the Pentagon earlier Tuesday, railed against Massie and defended his leadership in the Iran war and other military operations.

"What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said

"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," Hegseth said. "It puts a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time."This is not patriotism. This is sabotage."

Trump, in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, said Hegseth "gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!"

Trump said Monday that he would stand by Hegseth even if the House impeaches him. The president was impeached by the House two times during his first White House term. The Senate acquitted him in both cases.

Republicans hold a slim 218-214 majority in the House.

Some Republicans, notably including Vice President JD Vance, have directly blamed their midterm losses on the Iran war, which continues to see intermittent fighting amid an uneasy stalemate.

If Hegseth is impeached, the Senate would hold a trial and vote on whether to remove him from office. A two-thirds majority is required for conviction and removal.

No Cabinet secretary has ever been removed by the Senate. Just two have been impeached.

#2805. Koa Peat’s development requires patience amid Suns’ early struggles

You could feel it last night during the loss to the San Antonio Spurs, couldn't you? When Suns' rookie wing Koa Peat entered the game, you could feel that "disease of what if" beginning to creep in. Perhaps I felt it more than most because I'd spent my morning browsing eBay, looking through the newly released 2026-27 Topps basketball cards and hunting for Peat rookie cards. Side note: I love that they're doing the 45th anniversary of the 1981-82 Topps cards. Classically beautiful.

So when he entered the game with 5:56 left and the Suns trailing by 30 points in the fourth quarter, I suddenly had a reason to remain engaged for the rest of the evening. And he didn't disappoint. The first time Peat touched the ball, he attacked the cylinder, drove left, spun right, and banked a beautiful 6-foot shot off the glass for two points. On the very next possession, he found himself in transition and tossed an alley-oop to Michael Jordan reincarnated in Jamaree Bouyea for another two points.

I felt it deep within my soul. We need to get this guy minutes!

Then reality quickly set in. There aren't necessarily minutes available for him right now, and one of the primary reasons those two possessions looked so beautiful was sitting comfortably on the San Antonio bench. Victor Wembanyama, the very villain responsible for putting Phoenix in a 30-point hole, wasn't on the floor to swat either opportunity into the fifth row.

When you're watching a team that desperately lacks size and rebounding, any opportunity to see a player who possesses those attributes immediately feels like you've stumbled upon the solution. You begin convincing yourself that the coaching staff doesn't know what it's doing, that players like Peat should be receiving consistent opportunities because they offer something the current rotation is sorely missing.

On paper, that sounds wonderful. In reality, it's not nearly that simple, and there are legitimate reasons why it shouldn't happen right now.

For starters, where are those minutes supposed to come from? Ryan Dunn has been playing out of his mind to begin the season. Are we supposed to take some of his limited 16.7 minutes away? Do we cut his playing time in half so Peat can get on the floor long enough to work up a sweat without ever establishing enough rhythm to make those minutes meaningful?

Granted, if we could carve out some minutes from Jalen Green, I'd certainly entertain that conversation. Perhaps that's where an opportunity exists. But the reality is that developing chemistry and cohesion requires consistency within your rotations. You can't expect players to become comfortable with one another if you're constantly reshuffling responsibilities and playing time every time a rookie enters a game and strings together two positive possessions.

Quite honestly, if Peat is receiving significant minutes right now, it probably means the Suns have shifted their priorities away from winning in the present and toward developing for the future. As I've stated before, losing doesn't benefit this franchise. Phoenix doesn't control its own draft destiny, so intentionally prioritizing development at the expense of winning creates a situation where you're accumulating losses without receiving the traditional reward that comes with them. You might as well go out there and try to win basketball games.

There will eventually come a time when development becomes a greater priority. If the Suns remain 12th in the Western Conference standings as the season progresses, the organization may need to reevaluate its approach and provide more meaningful opportunities to its younger players. At that point, giving Peat, Fleming, and others additional minutes could become an important part of determining what the future looks like.

But we're nine games into the season. Nine. And while I recognize there are people already pounding their fists on the table demanding more playing time for Peat, I'm here to tell you that now is neither the time nor the place.

That's the challenge of the disease of what if. It sends your mind wandering toward hypothetical solutions that seem perfectly logical when you're watching your team get dismantled. You see a young player make a couple of exciting plays, recognize that he possesses attributes your team desperately needs, and begin imagining how differently things might have unfolded had he been given an opportunity earlier.

But countless variables contribute to those moments. The opponent's personnel, the score, the defensive intensity, the matchups, and the circumstances surrounding those opportunities all matter. And because you'll never receive a definitive answer to what would have happened had that player entered the game earlier, the hypothetical begins to feel like a solution.

Adding some fuel to the debate is that Suns' head coach Jordan Ott stated just a few days ago that Peat is "right on the cusp."

"Koa is next and Koa's right there on the tip," Ott stated. "We understand that he's young and he's hasn't done doesn't have a ton of NBA game experience, but again, the way the game is moving, the ability to drive, process, and defend the drive, he appears to have it, and he's right there. He'll get his opportunity, and we have full faith that that's what's coming."

The Suns could certainly use some help on the glass, as last night's loss served as another painful reminder of how difficult it has been for this team to secure rebounds. Phoenix was outrebounded by 20 against San Antonio and currently ranks dead last in the NBA with a 44.6% overall rebounding percentage. Perhaps even more concerning is its defensive rebounding percentage, which sits at a league-worst 60.1%. That means opposing teams have an alarmingly high likelihood of extending possessions by grabbing offensive rebounds, a recurring nightmare for Phoenix.

The consequences are showing up on the scoreboard. The Suns allow a league-high 19.0 second-chance points per game, essentially handing opponents additional scoring opportunities because they cannot consistently finish defensive possessions with a rebound. It's difficult enough to stop NBA offenses the first time around. When you're giving them multiple opportunities to score on the same possession, you're making an already challenging task nearly impossible.

Where do I land on Koa Peat? I want to see him play. I want to see what he can become, and I certainly want the Suns to develop the talent they've invested in. But wanting to see more of a player and believing he deserves more minutes right now are two different things.

The Suns have to balance the future with the present, and nine games into the season, they still have a responsibility to compete. Maybe Peat eventually earns a larger role. Maybe the circumstances change and create that opportunity. Until then, we have to resist the temptation to turn two exciting possessions into an answer to problems that are considerably more complicated. The disease of what if is powerful, but it doesn't necessarily make the prescription any better.

Me? I'll just head back over to eBay and hunt more rookie autos.

#2804. Schumer accuses Trump of defending Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at cost of national security

Democratic leader Sen. Charles Schumer ripped President Donald Trump on Tuesday for defending embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the expense of U.S. national security.

"The press reports that Trump was briefed more than a year ago that Nvidia's CEO was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and Trump didn't do anything – anything – about it," Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the Senate floor.

"Can you believe that?" said Schumer, the Senate's minority leader.

Schumer's broadside came on the heels of New York Times reports that Trump had been briefed about Huang's extramarital affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — whom U.S. intelligence concluded was a spy for China — and opted not to do anything about it.

Trump suggested to reporters on Monday that he only recently learned of the allegations about Alice Huang, and the president commented Monday that he "really" believes Jensen Huang's claim to him directly that he had no idea Alice Huang was a spy.

"One of our most important companies that is involved in national security, and the CEO might be having an affair with a Chinese spy, and Trump did nothing about it," Schumer said Tuesday.

"What a dereliction of duty. He's supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends," Schumer said. "Trump has been busy trying to defend Jensen Huang when he ought to be defending our national security. It's that simple, it's obvious."

Schumer's comments escalated growing bipartisan concern in Congress about the Nvidia CEO, whose company makes advanced chips that power artificial intelligence in the U.S. and China's race to dominate that technology.

Schumer noted that Trump earlier this year invited Huang to join him on a state visit to Beijing, and that he took Huang's advice by granting the People's Republic of China "access to some of our most advanced AI chips."

Nvidia also donated $25 million to Trump's controversial White House ballroom project, the Democrat said.

"Despite talking a big game, Trump continues to show a troubling resistance to confront China on AI and to protect American national security," Schumer said. "I've been saying it for years: our cutting-edge AI chips are too valuable to fall into the hands of potential adversaries."

Schumer in his speech called on Republicans to join Democrats in passing several pieces of legislation — the AI OVERWATCH Act, the MATCH Act, and the Chip Security Act — which he said would "cut off China's access to advanced American technology."

"We also need answers on Nvidia's influence campaign and how [it] affected the Trump administration's national security decisions, including the loosening – the loosening – of key export controls," Schumer said. "We need a full accounting for Trump's failure to address foreign espionage in the American tech industry."

CNBC has requested comment from the White House about Schumer's remarks.

The remarks came nearly a week after Democrats won enough Senate and House races nationwide to take majority control of both chambers in January. Schumer hopes to be selected majority leader.

Regardless of which Democrats are tapped to serve as majority leaders in both chambers, the party will have the ability to launch investigations into Nvidia and Huang.

Earlier Tuesday, Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" that Congress needs to "get to the bottom" of Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang.

Moolenaar, who chairs the House Permanent Select Committee on China, said he wants to know whether Huang shared privileged information with a Chinese spy; whether Huang was influenced to lobby against preventing chip sales to China; and whether China was given preference in purchasing Nvidia's limited supply of advanced chips.

And he urged a thorough internal investigation of Huang.

"If it becomes less of an investigation, more of damage control, that's not going to work because people have to have confidence," Moolenaar said.

"We're dealing with the country, the Chinese Communist Party that is a foremost adversary, that's funding wars and supporting Russia, supporting Iran, North Korea," he said. "And we have basically a Cold War race with technology. We cannot allow the premier company at the forefront of this to, in some way, be irresponsible."

Congressional scrutiny of Huang's affair has intensified since members returned to Washington on Monday, a day after Nvidia announced it was opening an independent investigation of Jensen Huang's conduct.

Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., co-chair of the House AI task force, raised concerns that the scandal could plague talks over export controls for advanced AI chips."It's important not to have a personal scandal interfere with the substantive policy discussion about to what degree we should be allowing the export of cutting edge chips to our geopolitical competitors like China," Obernolte told CNBC. "I hope this isn't a distraction because that's a very important conversation that needs to happen."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said in a press conference on Monday that "we're going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of national security"

Moolenaar co-authored a letter with Florida Rep. Brian Mast and Arkansas Rep. Rick Crawford on Nov. 5 asking Huang to appear before the Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee and House Select Committee on Intelligence. Mast chairs the foreign affairs panel, and Crawford chairs intelligence.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the three Republicans wrote.

Mast said Tuesday he did not know whether Huang had responded to the letter he authored with Moolenar and Crawford demanding the tech CEO brief them. "I can't say that I've heard an answer back yet that," Mast told reporters at the Capitol.Mast then rattled off a list of questions he has for Huang, including where the company has been selling chips, what Megaspeed may have been using them for, who has been remotely accessing Nvidia chips and what information was passed between Huang and the potential spy. "Obviously questions relating to his relationship and what information was or was not passed about anything," Mast said when asked what he wants answered.

Mast said he "can't say it would hurt" to hear from the Commerce Department as well, noting he speaks regularly to the Bureau of Industry and Security. "So that's obviously something that falls directly under Commerce," he said

#2803. Deion Sanders takes the blame for Colorado’s struggles with Buffs on brink of another losing season

BOULDER, Colo. (AP) — Deion Sanders is taking full responsibility with the Colorado Buffaloes on the brink of a third losing campaign in his fours seasons in Boulder.

The coach insisted over the weekend that he's not worried about getting fired — "I'm not built like that," he said — and reiterated Tuesday that the blame stops with him. He even caught himself midsentence in explaining the losses.

"We're just not getting it done. I'm just not getting it done," Sanders said. "Don't say we. I'm sorry. Scratch that. I'm not getting it done all the way around. All the way around. Offensive and defensively, special teams — all the way around."

The heat has been turned up several degrees on Sanders with the Buffaloes (3-6, 1-5 Big 12) struggling and needing to win their remaining three games for a chance at bowl eligibility. That starts Friday night with Colorado hosting No. 14 Houston (7-2, 4-2) and the Cougars a 10 1/2-point favorite.

Sanders, who is making a base salary of $10 million this year, is under contract through the 2029 season. His buyout hovers around $25.5 million. He has gone 6-15 since the departure of his son, quarterback Shedeur Sanders, and 2024 Heisman Trophy winner Travis Hunter to the NFL. Overall, Deion Sanders is 19-27 at Colorado.

"I don't flinch," Sanders said of how he handles the losses. "They know who I am and my expectations all the way across the board. This is not common to me. I don't like it. I don't enjoy it one bit. This is not indicative of who we think we are.

"I think the coordinators are doing a phenomenal job, the best they can. I think the kids are fighting. They would not give up. They don't have that gene in them, for the majority."

Sanders and his job status were brought up Saturday night after a 20-10 loss at Arizona State. He said he was not dwelling on it.

"I'm not here for my job. I'm here for these young men," he said after the game. "I want these kids to graduate, to provoke change in their communities, in their lives and their families. I ain't not worried about me. I'm good. I'm not worried about me."

One of the biggest stumbling blocks this season has been getting the offense in rhythm. The team is averaging a conference-low 19.8 points a game in the "Go-Go" offense, a fast-paced scheme brought to town by coordinator Brennan Marion.

Any thought of possibly replacing the play-caller?

After more questions on Marion, Sanders responded: "Is this Killing Brennan Day, today?"

Sanders wasn't entertaining the notion that an offseason could potentially help sort out an offense that's seen QB Julian "JuJu" Lewis and Isaac Wilson at the helm.

"We're thinking about day-by-day, play-by-play, game-by-game," Sanders said. "I'm not built like that. I'm a now guy. Let's focus on now."

"We're still trying to fight for a chance to get in the bowl game," receiver DeAndre Moore Jr. said. "We just have to come in with the mindset of continuing to get better."

NOTES: Sanders was sweating at his weekly news conference after playing a little safety in practice Tuesday as part of the scout team. "I think I had nine tackles, three assists, couple of pass breakups," the Hall of Fame defensive back playfully said. "I have fun doing it, and I'm getting my cardio in as well." ... Colorado linebacker Gideon ESPN Lampron won his second straight Big 12 defensive player of the week award. He had 18 tackles and two sacks at Arizona State. "Gideon plays hard every day in practice, and he takes it right over into the game," Sanders said. ... The defense is allowing 28.3 points a game.

#2801. LeBron Log No. 4: A courtside sip, 16,000 makes and Cleveland's welcome

LeBron Log No. 4: A courtside sip, 16,000 makes and Cleveland's welcome originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James' latest week with the Sixers included a sip of a stranger's wine, yet another number no NBA player had reached and a return to the city where his career began.

It also included his worst performance with Philadelphia, followed less than 48 hours later by his highest-scoring game with the team.

Welcome to the fourth edition of the LeBron Log.

No chronicle of James' first season in Philadelphia could omit the time he helped himself to a fan's wine during a game.

James chased Tyrese Maxey's transition pass into the stands during the third quarter of the Sixers' Nov. 2 win over the Bulls. He collided with Philadelphia native Troy Clemons, spilled some of Clemons' wine and sampled what had landed on his arm.

The interaction received its own story on our site, and deservedly so. It also belongs in the Log.

Clemons did not keep the cup as a souvenir. He threw it away and got another drink.

James returned to the court and later broke into a dance after scoring over the 6-foot-1 Tre Jones. The wine clip generated millions of views across social media and became the defining image from an otherwise ordinary 19-point Sixers victory.

The following night in Detroit, James offered a broader explanation for why Philadelphia has already looked comfortable together.

"We've got a good team," James said. "Guys vibe with one another. Guys like each other. Guys enjoy being around each other. That has a lot to do with it, too. It makes the game a lot easier when you enjoy being around people."

Eleven games into his Sixers career, James appears to be doing exactly that.

James arrived in Detroit two baskets away from another unprecedented number.

His second field goal against the Pistons made him the first player in NBA history to reach 16,000 regular-season field goals.

James finished the Sixers' 112-106 victory with 13 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists. The near-triple-double helped Philadelphia improve to 8-1 and avenge its only loss of the season.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar ranks second in league history with 15,837 made field goals. Karl Malone is a distant third at 13,528. James is the only active player with more than 12,000.

His scoring record has long been secure. James passed Abdul-Jabbar in career points in February 2023 and later overtook him in made baskets. The round number in Detroit still illustrated the distance he has created between himself and every other scorer.

James began his career by making 5,361 field goals across seven seasons with Cleveland. He added 3,510 in Miami, returned to make 3,691 more for the Cavaliers and made another 3,421 during eight years with the Lakers.

Basket No. 16,000 belonged to Philadelphia.

The Sixers' 8-1 start also carried a notable James connection. Each of his previous four teams to begin a season at least 7-1 reached the NBA Finals.

James was not ready to entertain that conversation in early November.

"It's too early to be talking about the Finals and things of that nature," he said. "We've got to continue to buy into what we want to do."

Two nights later, James returned to the place where nearly half of those 16,000 baskets were made.

His first game in Cleveland as a Sixer brought out jerseys from every stop of his career. Cavaliers colors filled Rocket Arena alongside Heat black, Lakers purple and the Sixers' throwback look.

James received a warm ovation when he was introduced last among Philadelphia's starters. When he checked out late in the fourth quarter, with the result decided, the crowd stood for him again.

James has experienced both ends of Cleveland's emotional range.

He returned as a member of the Heat on Dec. 2, 2010, to one of the most hostile receptions in NBA history. Six years later, he delivered the Cavaliers their first championship and ended Cleveland's 52-year major professional sports title drought.

"I've seen the depths of hell when it comes to a reception here, all the way to the heavens above," James said. "Anything in between is easy money."

The reception fell somewhere in the middle. His performance landed much closer to the bottom.

James finished with eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, three assists and six turnovers in the Sixers' 119-95 loss. It was his first single-digit performance in Cleveland since he scored three points against the Rockets on Dec. 30, 2004.

He had scored at least 10 points in 396 consecutive regular-season games in the city. The run covered his first stint with the Cavaliers, every visit as an opponent and his entire second tenure with the organization.

It ended during his first trip back in a Sixers uniform.

"I definitely did not feel in a good rhythm offensively," James said. "A couple of them were careless. A couple of them were just trying to make the right play and not being successful with it."

It was only the 10th single-digit regular-season game of James' 1,630-game career. He still took time afterward to consider what an eventual jersey retirement in Cleveland could represent.

"The journey from being an 18-year-old rookie, to leading a franchise to a championship," James said. "And everything in between."

James did not carry the rough night into Chicago.

Less than 48 hours after struggling in Cleveland, he scored a season-high 22 points in the Sixers' 127-121 victory over the Bulls. Thirteen came during the second quarter, when James helped Philadelphia turn an early deficit into a halftime lead.

His first basket produced another milestone.

James entered Sunday trailing Abdul-Jabbar's 1,895 points for the most scored against the Bulls in NBA history. His first-quarter three-pointer moved him into the lead. He ended the afternoon with 1,916.

The most interesting play from his night was a pass.

With the Sixers ahead by four and 2:20 remaining, James drove into the paint. Three Chicago defenders collapsed toward him. Maxey stood between the left wing and corner, but even he did not believe James could see him.

James fired the ball through the defense. Maxey sidestepped Isaac Okoro and made the three-pointer, pushing Philadelphia's lead to seven.

After his postgame interview, James pulled out his phone and watched the play again.

"He didn't think I saw him," James called out from his locker as reporters asked Maxey about the possession.

Maxey acknowledged that he had positioned himself to rebound because he expected James to shoot.

"Honestly, I was like this," Maxey said, raising his hands. "I thought he was about to shoot a layup."

James has spent the opening weeks of the season teaching his new teammates to expect the unexpected pass.

"You've got to become a wide receiver or a catcher at that point," Maxey said. "You never know when you're going to get the ball.

#2800. Manchester United’s Jacob Devaney nominated for international player of the year award

Manchester United's Jacob Devaney has been nominated for an award at the 36th Football Association of Ireland (FAI) International Awards.

The youngster has been recognised for his performances in the green of Ireland and has been named to a three-man shortlist for Ireland's U21s player of the year.

He has been nominated alongside Tottenham Hotspur's (on loan at Lincoln City) Mason Melia and Wycombe Wanderers' Jamie Mullins.

The award has previously been won by Manchester United academy graduates Robbie Brady and Lee O'Connor. Perhaps the most recognisable winner of the award is Jack Grealish, who switched allegiance shortly after to represent England.

Devaney has made 12 appearances for Ireland U21s, with the most recent coming in a thrilling 3-1 victory over England that sealed a play-off berth for the 2027 U21s European Championship.

The midfielder has been named in Ireland's squad for the upcoming play-off double-header against Finland, which could see Ireland qualify for the U21s Euros for the first time ever.

He also recently captained his country in a friendly against Qatar U21s, an honour he has held with United's U21s as well.

After a stellar loan last season at St. Mirren, Devaney impressed on United's pre-season tour with a goal against Rosenborg BK but did not get a chance to show his full potential, being played out of position at centre-back rather than his more natural central midfield role.

A combative, press-resistant midfielder, Devaney's consistency and versatility make him an asset to any team and could prove important to United's lack of depth in the future.

The award nomination will provide confidence to the 19-year-old as he looks to get back on track after a rocky start to the season.

Looking to build upon his successful loan last season, Devaney returned to Scotland, moving up the table to Hibernian.

Devaney went straight into their starting XI, but a string of poor results to start the season actually sees them lying below St. Mirren in the table and, as a result, the manager who brought him to the club was sacked.

In his first appearance under the new manager, Marink Reedijk, Devaney unfortunately picked up a straight red card just seven minutes after being introduced from the bench.

To make matters worse, the red card challenge actually resulted in him getting injured, which has kept him out ever since.

The Midlothian View report that Devaney is nearing a return from injury, but he'll need to impress Reedijk, who has said, "this is the difficulty for me because I've seen Jacob for two training sessions and five minutes on the pitch in Dundee. And after that, I haven't seen him and worked with him."

"Off the pitch, I have an idea of who he is as a person. But now I also want to see how he brings this to the pitch. And this I cannot judge on yet."

Devaney's return starts with Ireland U21s, though, and a potential player of the year award which will bring him the confidence to kick on and perhaps earn a spot back at United next season.

#2799. Raiders rookie QB Fernando Mendoza in line to make first career start vs. Seahawks after Kirk Cousins trade

Fernando Mendoza, a reigning national champion, is poised to face the defending Super Bowl champions in his first career NFL start.

Mendoza, who led Indiana on a storybook run to College Football Playoff glory, is in line to get the nod for the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday at Allegiant Stadium against the Seattle Seahawks.

He's up for a 4-5 Raiders team that traded veteran Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a 2027 third-round pick hours before Tuesday's trade deadline. That deal effectively marked the beginning of the Mendoza era in Vegas.

After learning under the 38-year-old Cousins before and during the season, the 23-year-old Mendoza is set for quite the three-game test leading up to the Raiders' Week 13 bye.

Not only will he have to face the Seahawks' vaunted defense, but he'll have to go up against the Denver Broncos and Cleveland Browns the subsequent two weeks. Entering Week 10, all three of those teams rank inside the top 13 in fewest points per game allowed this season. The Broncos and Browns are tied with a handful of teams for fourth in the NFL with 26 sacks.

Mendoza has attempted only eight regular-season passes. All of those came in relief of Cousins down the stretch of a 45-17 road loss to the New England Patriots. That was part of a four-game Raiders skid that followed their head-turning 3-0 start.

First-year head coach Klint Kubiak, who named Cousins the team's Week 1 starter after evaluating both him and Mendoza in the preseason, stuck with Cousins under center despite the October losing streak.

Cousins was open throughout his stay in Las Vegas that he was well aware of the circumstances of his role and that his time as Raiders QB1 was limited. He stressed that he wanted to put the team in the best position to win games, even if that meant at some point handing the baton to Mendoza.

But Cousins played so well that he kept his job leading up to the deadline. In fact, an ESPN report surfaced this past Sunday morning, detailing how, at the time, the Raiders weren't interested in dealing him.

Cousins turned back the clock while working with Kubiak, posting a 20:8 touchdown-to-interception ratio. His 20 TD passes are good for second-most in the league and signify his first season with at least that many since his 2022 campaign with the Vikings, with whom he played from 2018-23.

Cousins turned out to be among the best NFL rentals in recent memory. The Raiders paid him a total of $650,000, per ESPN's Field Yates, and his value resulted in a third-round pick and priceless mentorship.

He appeared to forge an endearing friendship with Mendoza, who eagerly absorbed tips and tricks from Cousins.

Las Vegas drafted Mendoza first overall in the aftermath of his prolific 2025 season with the Hoosiers. He won the Heisman Trophy, vaulted himself into the end zone en route to beating Miami in the national championship and finished the season with 48 total touchdowns, including 41 through the air.

His effervescence, often on full display in postgame interviews, made him a unique college football star. He's still that happy-go-lucky QB, at least outside the white lines.

Time will tell how his game translates to NFL regular-season play. He completed six of his eight passes against the Patriots for 48 yards. In the preseason, he had mixed results, impressing in his debut against the Arizona Cardinals and then throwing a pick-6 versus the Houston Texans and another interception against the San Francisco 49ers.

Mendoza wrapped the preseason, according to Pro Football Focus, with 250 yards on 26-of-46 passing, registering a 56.5% completion rate, one touchdown pass and those two picks.

It's been months since then, however. The Cousins trade speaks to Minnesota's desperation for a quarterback solution, but it also says a lot about the Raiders' trust in Mendoza's development.
