#2798. A massive trade in Nvidia just went off – here are the details

The biggest options trade on Nvidia stock Monday seems to think the controversy swirling around the chip leader and its embattled CEO is creating a buying opportunity.In a trade about an hour after the opening bell that involved more than $100 million in options premium, someone exchanged an existing call spread for a more bullish position that captures the next five months of trading in Nvidia.The core position was the purchase of 52,000 195-strike calls expiring Feb. 19 worth about $57 million – contracts the trader opened for a new long position while simultaneously selling the same number of 245-strike calls for the same expiry, lowering the cost of the trade by $10 million. The net position, a bullish call spread, needs Nvidia to trade above around $206 by expiry, or about 15% higher, to be profitable. If Nvidia stock reaches the short, 245-strike call, it would represent a nearly 40% rally and return the stock to its all-time high of $243, that was reached on October 6th.The trade was likely part of a "roll" down from an existing 210/255-strike call spread worth about $42 million that was closed out, according to SpotGamma analysis.

"The person got more aggressive rolling this spread down to lower strikes to get more upside exposure by getting higher delta," SpotGamma founder Brent Kochuba said by phone. "They're trading the call spread here because the vol is expensive going into earnings. It's a significant increase in upside delta exposure."Delta is options parlance for describing how quickly an options price will react to a change in the underlying stock price. The trader's updated position, taken at lower strikes, will make money faster if Nvidia rallies. In other words, it's a higher conviction trade that the chipmaker's stock will soon rebound. The 195-strike calls they bought for $57 million was the single biggest options trade on the tape Monday, according to SpotGamma. Of the top 20 options trades by dollar-amount, 12 were Nvidia, the data show.Flows around the stock generally leaned bullish by midday, with 57% of options volume tied to calls and more than $660 million of call premium likely initiated by call-buyers, SpotGamma data show. The most popular single contract by volume was the 180-strike call expiring Monday, that needs Nvidia to recover 1.2% by the bell to break even.

#2797. Not many players are truly untradeable

In recent days (including today), reports have emerged that certain players will not be traded. That definitely does not mean they’re untradeable.

It means only that the team has yet to get an offer it will accept. The mere process of working the insiders to send that message could give the process one final goosing.

Regardless, not many players are truly untradeable. For all but a handful of players, there’s an offer that his current team would accept.

The only players who currently wouldn’t be traded, in our view, are Bills quarterback Josh Allen, Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow, Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, Bears quarterback Caleb Williams, Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence, Packers quarterback Jordan Love, and probably 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy.

Any other can be had, at the right offer (up to and including three first-round picks plus more). By now, teams know whether the right offer will be made. Which makes it easy for them to throw out their chests and say the player won’t be traded.

And to reverse course if an offer they can’t refuse is made before 4:00 p.m. ET today.

#2796. Observations after well-balanced Sixers hold off Bulls

Observations after well-balanced Sixers hold off Bulls originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Still no losing streaks to speak of for the 2026-27 Sixers.

The Sixers earned a 127-121 win Sunday over the Bulls to wrap up a 2-1 road trip. They moved to 9-2 overall and Chicago fell to 1-8.

Every Sixers starter scored in double figures.

Three reached the 20-point mark in Jaylen Brown (29 points), Tyrese Maxey (27 points) and LeBron James (22). Joel Embiid had 18 points and 10 rebounds.

Josh Giddey posted 19 points, 15 assists and seven rebounds for the Bulls.

The Sixers were without Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear). The Bulls' absences included Norman Powell (right shoulder inflammation/soreness) and Zach Collins (respiratory illness).

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a home game Tuesday night vs. the Celtics. Here are observations on their win over Chicago:

Following his 0-for-9 night Friday in the Sixers' loss to the Cavaliers, Embiid did not snap right back into form.

He was well short on his first shot attempt, a wide-open three-pointer. Embiid then failed to score in the post over Jalen Smith.

Embiid got a field goal to go at the 6:42 mark of the first quarter when he tipped in his own miss. However, Smith canned a three on the ensuing possession to give Chicago a 23-16 lead.

James committed two early turnovers, although he did sink a corner three-pointer during a fast-paced first quarter. VJ Edgecombe added two long-range jumpers in the first.

Entering Sunday, the Sixers' minus-9.6 net rating in the first quarter ranked 27th in the NBA. They managed to hold a one-point lead in Chicago after the first.

The Sixers' offensive rebounding was their greatest strength in the first quarter. They poured in 17 second-chance points. Embiid had four offensive boards in the opening frame.

Jabari Walker assumed backup center duties for the second straight game without Bona. He picked up where Embiid left off on the glass, grabbing seven rebounds (three offensive) in a great first stint.

Though he's undersized in the height department for an NBA center at 6-foot-7, Walker has plenty of rebounding tools.

He's listed at a strong 237 pounds, doesn't mind contact whatsoever, hunts the ball, and has a knack for winning contested boards. Walker showed all of that Sunday. Very hard to overstate how well he rebounded.

The Sixers' first-shot offense also had many bright moments in the second quarter.

James got rolling on his way to a 16-point first half, Embiid made a couple of mid-range jumpers, and Maxey hit two free throws put the Sixers up 60-50 late in the second period.

Chicago evened the game at 68-all early in the third quarter on a Matas Buzelis three, but the Bulls couldn't sustain that run.

The Bulls' defense continued to look like one of the worst in the NBA and the Sixers' well-balanced offense kept the scoreboard moving. Brown nailed a turnaround jumper to give his team a double-digit lead. Walker knocked down a top-of-the-key triple to extend the Sixers' advantage to 12 points.

The Sixers had two apparent injury scares in the second half. Brown limped to the sideline with 6:55 to go in the third quarter, but he stayed in the game. Edgecombe headed to the locker room after subbing out at the 9:08 mark of the fourth quarter. He returned to the Sixers' bench and ultimately returned for a final stint.

On the floor, the Sixers couldn't ease to victory. Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson trimmed Chicago's deficit to 116-113 by draining a three. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse called timeout.

The Sixers were efficient enough in the half court down the stretch.

Embiid made a put-back hoop and a pair of free throws. Maxey drilled a side-step three-ball after a wraparound feed from James. The Sixers converted their clutch free throws and secured a winning road trip.

#2794. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2790. Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup

Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers couldn't rekindle the magic of their comeback home-opening win over the Cavaliers.

They fell Friday night in NBA Cup action, suffering a 119-95 defeat in Cleveland. The Sixers dipped to 8-2 and the Cavs improved to 5-4.

The Sixers' top scorers were Jaylen Brown (20 points), VJ Edgecombe (19 points) and Tyrese Maxey (17).

The Cavs got 23 points from Donovan Mitchell and 22 from Evan Mobley.

The Sixers' injured players included center Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain). Cleveland was down big man Jarrett Allen (right knee contusion). Sam Merrill sat out the second half with a right elbow injury.

With Friday's loss, the Sixers are 1-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup. Their next Cup game is scheduled for Nov. 25 against the Heat.

The Sixers will conclude their three-road trip Sunday afternoon against the Bulls. Here are observations on their blowout loss to Cleveland:

After a missed Merrill three-pointer, the Sixers steamed ahead on the fast break and Edgecombe opened the scoring with a slam.

The Cavs replied with a 15-0 run kickstarted by six straight Mitchell points. Much like in the Sixers' Oct. 22 win over Cleveland, they were many levels below their best in the first quarter.

The Sixers began 0 for 4 from three-point range, including two LeBron James misses. The Cavs were also the better team in transition and limited the Sixers' chances to attack in the open floor by taking excellent care of the ball in the early going. Edgecombe was called for his second foul with 7:34 left in the first quarter.

Meanwhile, Joel Embiid expressed his frustration about a couple of early no-calls. Embiid's larger problem was that he couldn't hit any sort of shot besides free throws.

He went 0 for 9 from the floor in the game. The seven-time All-Star finished with six points and seven rebounds.

Embiid has had a subpar shooting start to the year, especially from three-point territory — he's now 3 for 28 (10.7 percent) — but Friday was the kind of extreme night that's bound to happen here and there over the course of a long season.

Of course, it's notable that Embiid's been playing through right foot plantar fasciitis and the Sixers have been keeping a close eye on his minutes. We'll see how the team manages his availability moving forward and whether Embiid is able to bounce back next time out.

James didn't play anywhere near his finest game either. He had eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, eight rebounds, three assists and six turnovers.

As a team, the Sixers were 36.5 percent from the field and 25 percent beyond the arc.

Jabari Walker rejoined the Sixers' rotation as the backup center with Bona sidelined. Anfernee Simons, former Cav Dean Wade and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope all remained rotation fixtures.

With Walker and Caldwell-Pope on the court next to three starters, the Sixers cut their deficit to single digits in the second quarter. Walker threw down a fast-break dunk that cut Cleveland's lead to 48-41. He gave the Sixers some good defensive possessions when switched on to James Harden and provided his usual physical, high-effort work on the glass.

Edgecombe was fantastic in the second, sinking three triples, racking up 15 points and nabbing three steals.

Many second-year players would have a tough time finding a rhythm after encountering early foul trouble, but Edgecombe was great as soon as he checked back in and delivered a ton of valuable buckets in the Sixers' comeback push.

The Sixers pulled to within 66-63 when Maxey picked a steal and threw a pretty one-handed bounce pass to Edgecombe for a dunk.

With Embiid and James offering little as scorers, Brown hit several shots that helped the Sixers stay in the game. After his 30-point performance last time out against the Pistons, Brown reached the 20-point mark for a third consecutive game.

Still, the Sixers' offense never got rolling. The Cavs maintained their lead and extended it late in the third quarter. By early in the fourth, the Sixers trailed by over 20 points.

Embiid didn't play the fourth quarter and logged 25 minutes. He's had zero made field goals on just one other occasion in his career, back in Nov. 2019 against the Raptors.

Even with their tremendous first nine games, the Sixers knew they'd hit speed bumps throughout the year. They'll try to get back on track Sunday in Chicago.

#2789. CoreWeave earnings put debt-fueled AI build-out under scrutiny

CoreWeave faces a pivotal test when it reports its third-quarter financial results after the bell on Tuesday.

The market will be closely watching what the neocloud company says about artificial intelligence spending — and how it plans to finance its infrastructure buildout. The outcome could either calm concerns over its debt or stoke more fear.

"Investors need neoclouds to quantify how much financing they expect to raise to execute on existing backlog," Wolfe Research said in a note Monday. "We think outlooks that communicate when and which avenues of funding will be tapped will increase investor confidence."

CoreWeave stock and bonds have come under pressure as fears deepened about the enormous amount of debt it has taken out to build its data centers.

Its stock is down roughly 40% over the past month. Meanwhile, the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 15.5% on Tuesday, after jumping to 16.7% on Thursday as investors digested the election results and possible roadblocks to data center construction. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

The spread on its five-year credit default swaps — which is insurance against default and considered a barometer of perceived credit risk — is also at levels that are considered distressed. On Tuesday, its CDS spread stood around 1,152 basis points, after rising above its October peak to close at 1,278 basis points on Thursday. Rising CDS spreads mean investors view the debt as riskier.

In addition, the New Jersey-based company's leverage is high. CoreWeave has a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from almost 291% a year ago.

CEO Michael Intrator has sought to quell investor fear, posting on LinkedIn after the election last week that the company doesn't anticipate "any impact to CoreWeave's existing customer commitments or associated backlog as a result of shifts in the political landscape."

The company reported a revenue backlog of $104.2 billion in the second quarter. It has about $35 billion in debt, as of June 30.

CoreWeave has already given a picture of what it expects for the third quarter.

It guided for quarterly revenue of $3.4 billion to $3.6 billion when it reported second-quarter results in August. It anticipated capital expenditures between $11.5 billion and $13.5 billion for the quarter and $35 billion to $39 billion for the full year. The company also expects 1.85 gigawatts in active power by year-end.

Wells Fargo expects the company's capex needs for the rest of the year to be largely covered by its remaining undrawn debt, debt issuances in August/September and the $12 billion it is holding for project costs, which will flow into capex, analyst Michael Turrin said in a note Sunday.

However, its 2027 capex could reach $66 billion, based on an expected capacity addition of 1.5 gigawatts, Turrin said. That will require at least $25 billion more in debt, he noted. It can be largely funded through delayed draw term loans, which allows CoreWeave to draw down funds over time, and the rest can come through bonds and convertibles, he said.

Turrin has an overweight rating and $115 price target on the stock, implying 135% upside from Monday's close.

"While neoclouds sit in the eye of the AI storm, we remain confident that CRWV is the highest quality co in the space," Turrin wrote. "Beyond the noise, we see capacity/revs coming in better than expected (1.95GW this yr vs guide 1.85GW) as margins start to inflect."

However, investors likely won't get all the answers they're seeking during CoreWeave's third-quarter results, said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin.

"One of the major issues for CoreWeave is whether or not they can obtain all the financing they need," he said. "They may try and calm the markets, but I'm not sure how much color they can and will provide."

Investors will be looking for 2027 guidance on capex and free cash flow, though that may not come until Coreweave releases fourth quarter results, Chalfin notes.

CoreWeave could ease investor concerns by showing it has plans and approvals in place to scale capacity through 2027, he said. The company can also demonstrate remaining performance obligation (RPO) growth, which shows the total value of its contracted future revenue, and highlight new customer wins.

In addition, pricing has been really strong on recent deals, Chalfin pointed out. "That could show up in an operating margin beat for Q3 and expectations for Q4."

While CoreWeave faces finances challenges, the company has many ways to access capital, Chalfin said. That includes chip-backed deals, which allow Corewave to borrow money using GPUs as collateral, and original equipment manufacturer financing. For instance, CoreWeave could turn to Dell, which is a big supplier with a strong balance sheet, Chalfin noted.

"Despite all the market sentiment, fundamentals are actually quite strong and pricing is strong," he said. "The trends over the next few quarters, I think, should be supportive." Risks could arise after that, but it is "too early to call."

Some analysts remain skeptical that Coreweave will be able to calm credit fears.

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, points out that the company is facing a huge bill in just over two years. CoreWeave owes roughly $15 billion in principal payments through 2028, according to its second-quarter earnings statement.

"They don't have enough cash to service all that debt," he said. "Unless some big orders come in, unless some big money flows come in for them in the next 17, 18 months, I think this is going to be the start of the end for CoreWeave, unless somebody comes in and wants to buy them. But who wants to buy all that debt?"

However, there could be a "small" window for the company to push out its debt for another three to five years, but it will depend on how strong their cash flow is when they report on Tuesday, Lang said.

Plus, issuing equity to help fund infrastructure projects, like Meta and Oracle did recently, isn't an option for CoreWeave, he noted.

"They're going to dilute the stock so much that it's going to continue to go down," he said. "They missed that window when the stock was in the hundreds."

CoreWeave topped $183 in June 2025. It has since declined more than 73%, recently trading around $47.

Despite the fall, analysts remain bullish on the stock with an average overweight rating and $126 target, based on 39 estimates complied by FactSet.

—CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed reporting.

#2787. 6 winners and losers from the Patriots’ trade deadline inactivity

The 2026 NFL trade deadline saw some big moves being made, but the New England Patriots did not join the fun. The team of head coach Mike Vrabel instead decided to let the Tuesday afternoon deadline come and go without either acquiring any players from the outside or moving on from some of their current personnel.

As a consequence, the roster will largely stay intact heading toward a Week 10 matchup with the Detroit Lions in Munich. Who can be seen as the primary benefactors of that inactivity, though? Here are some names that come to mind.

RB Corey Kiner and RB Lan Larison: With Rhamondre Stevenson reportedly set to miss time due to a knee injury, and with TreVeyon Henderson sidelined because of an illness, the Patriots adding some running back depth ahead of the deadline would not have come as too big of a surprise. The Colts' Jonathan Taylor or the Ravens' Derrick Henry were among the names mentioned as potential candidate, but even players with lesser star power would have negatively impacted the current group of backups. However, no trade happening can be seen as a vote of confidence in the likes of Corey Kiner and Lan Larison.

DT Christian Barmore: For starters, Carlton Davis getting traded always felt more like media speculation than anything else, so we are not going to spend much time on him. Christian Barmore, on the hand, could have changed teams had an attractive offer come along. It didn't meaning that he will stay put for the time being. Of course, Barmore's long-term outlook beyond the 2026 is still uncertain: while he can be a disruptive player and is currently ranked fifth on the Patriots with 15 quarterback pressures, he also is primarily a passing-down player that is being paid like a three-down contributor.

ED Harold Landry III, maybe: Pre-deadline rumors mentioned the Patriots as a potential landing spot for an edge rusher to complement a depth chart currently led by Dre'Mont Jones, Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas. No extra players being brought aboard means that the trio will continue leading the charge, but also that New England does feel at least good enough about its depth and positional outlook not to invest any extra resources in bolstering the group. One could interpret this as positive news for one player in particular: Harold Landry, who remains on the PUP list but is a candidate to be reactivated for the Patriots' home stretch. If the team felt uncertain about his ability to return at one point, it might have been more aggressive pursuing depth at the spot.

Depth receivers: A.J. Brown is nearing a return, but his latest absence due to a knee issue showed that the Patriots' wide receiver group is thin especially at the perimeter; Kyle Williams, the next man up, did little with the extended opportunity he received over the last two weeks and during Brown's previous stint on IR with a sprained ankle. Still, no outside help being added is good news for him and fellow depth receiver Efton Chism. The same is true for the depth at tight end, where Cameron Latu remains the de facto TE3 now that New England opted against bolstering his position group.

Receiver depth (and more): Of course, while the Patriots forgoing making any moves is good news for the individual players not negatively affected, it also means that the questions coming out of the Week 9 loss to the Packers remain. Kyle Williams is still the next man up at wide receiver, and Cameron Latu possibly one snap away from meaningful offensive playing time. Likewise, the Patriots' best-case scenario at right guard remains their second-stringer being able to return to the 53-man roster off of injured reserve. They also are putting a lot of trust in those aforementioned Corey Kiner and Lan Larison, the three-player edge rotation, and other positions who could on paper have benefitted from some fresh talent.

Next men up: Christian Barmore not getting traded suggests that the Patriots' status quo at defensive tackle will not change: Barmore is still a top-three guy alongside Milton Williams and Cory Durden. Had he been removed from the mix, the depth options — with Leonard Taylor probably the first name worth mentioning — would have been given more high-quality opportunities in the rotation.

#2785. Back in Philadelphia with Celtics, Paul George looks forward to ‘a regular game'

Back in Philadelphia with Celtics, Paul George looks forward to 'a regular game' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Paul George's presence back in town was one of the many swirling morning storylines at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

For good reason, former Celtics teammates Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum will draw immense attention Tuesday night. After all, Brown has said there "might be a little lamb chops with some gravy" between the two, if not a full-blown beef.

But George's return to Philadelphia is more than a tiny subplot. Following two seasons in Philadelphia, he was the centerpiece of the Sixers' summer trade package to acquire Brown.

George told reporters before the Celtics' shootaround that it feels like "a regular game."

"Had I been here eight, nine, 10 years, different story," he said. "I was here two years. Obviously, we didn't have the best of luck or had a great, I think, partnership in terms of my ability to stay healthy and on the floor. So that kind of played into a lot of it.

"But obviously, it's a tremendous fan base, a great sports town to play in. So that was appreciated. There's no ill will for me. It'll be fun to just compete. And outside of that, it's a normal game."

The 36-year-old George indeed had trouble staying available for sustained stretches as a Sixer. He dealt with a variety of injuries and served a 25-game suspension last season for violating the NBA's anti-drug policy.

George did play well on both ends of the floor for much of the 2026 playoffs. He helped the Sixers come back to win a seven-game first-round series against the Celtics in historic fashion. The nine-time All-Star also brought a veteran steadiness to the Sixers' locker room and was glad to mentor younger players like VJ Edgecombe.

"Just his routine … even when he got hot, he didn't try to force it," Jabari Walker said Tuesday morning. "His game was smooth and I think that's how he is as a person, just not forcing anything and having a calm energy."

George has certainly enjoyed his early days as a Celtic.

Through nine games, he's averaged 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 2.3 steals while shooting 42.5 percent from three-point range. Boston will enter Tuesday night's matchup second in the Eastern Conference standings at 8-2, the Sixers first at 9-2.

"I've been kind of blown away," George said. "I think it exceeded my expectations since being in Boston. You never know how much culture is involved and how much culture changes your outlook on things and the effect it has mentally, physically, just being in an environment … and the culture that Boston presents.

"So I've been thrilled. I've been playing some of my best basketball of late, and just been enjoying grinding it out with these guys out here. It's a fun style of play and I can't talk (enough) about just the thrill, the happiness and the excitement and joy that it has brought being here."

He was asked what sort of reception he expects from Sixers fans.

"Not sure," George said. "In some ways, I helped land them a future piece for them. So with that, not sure how the reception would be."

#2784. Broncos salary cap update after acquiring Daiyan Henley's contract

Going into the 2026 NFL trade deadline, OverTheCap.com estimated the Denver Broncos had about $4.6 million in available salary cap space.

The Broncos then agreed to trade a pair of draft picks to the Los Angeles Chargers in exchange for inside linebacker Daiyan Henley. With that trade, Denver inherited what's left of the fourth and final year of Henley's rookie contract, about $1.837 million for the second half of the season.

So, after accounting for Henley's cap hit of just over $1.8 million, the Broncos have something in the ballpark of about $2,765,451 in remaining cap space this season. Denver will have to keep a cushion for potential in-season signings and the possibility of players landing on injured reserve and still counting against the cap.

Any unused salary cap space the Broncos do not use this season will roll over and add to the team's 2027 total. OTC currently projects Denver will have about $30.46 million available next offseason.

#2779. ‘Let's check the ball up': Jaylen Brown ready for first game against Celtics

'Let's check the ball up': Jaylen Brown ready for first game against Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Jaylen Brown was asked Sunday whether he and Jayson Tatum had spoken since the former teammates addressed their relationship during the preseason.

Does he plan to approach Tatum before Tuesday night's game at Xfinity Mobile Arena?

"I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said. "We're playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win. So it's nothing to talk about. Let's check the ball up."

After months of public comments, documentaries and questions about how their partnership ended, the basketball will finally take over.

Brown will face Boston for the first time since the Celtics traded him to Philadelphia for Paul George and four future draft assets in July. He spent his first 10 NBA seasons in Boston, played nine alongside Tatum and helped the Celtics win the 2024 championship, earning Finals MVP honors.

Tuesday's 8 p.m. game on NBC will also bring together the top two teams in the Eastern Conference. The Sixers are 9-2. Boston, riding a three-game winning streak, is 8-2 and sits a half-game behind Philadelphia.

"Another good opportunity for our team to be able to show what we're made of," Brown said. "I'm looking forward to it. Big-time matchup, two heavyweights in the East. Let's get it."

Brown has not hidden his appreciation for Boston, even as more has emerged about the deterioration of his relationship with Tatum and the organization.

"I love Boston," he said Sunday. "Boston's a great city. A lot of people I developed relationships with, you know what I mean? But I'm just focused on what's in front of me right now. And that's the most important thing."

He also acknowledged everything that accompanies an abrupt end to a decade with one organization.

"Decisions were made," Brown said. "It's life. It's business. Move on. It's OK. … It's emotions. You've got to pack up and move your stuff. Your family's got to pack up and move. But it's life. It's happened to numerous amounts of people, myself included.

"So I just look forward to being able to build with my team over here, trying to make the best of my situation."

Brown faced the Celtics during the preseason, but Tuesday will be the first meeting that counts. He said he did not know whether that would introduce emotions that were absent during the exhibition schedule.

"We'll see how I feel when we get out there," Brown said. "As of now, I've got no emotion toward nothing. So I'm just ready to go."

Tatum was similarly restrained after Boston's 117-97 victory over Milwaukee on Sunday.

"It's another game on the schedule," Tatum said. "It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one."

Tatum called the Sixers "an incredible group" with a "great coaching staff," but declined to add to the discussion surrounding his relationship with Brown.

"Drama gets clicks and views," he said. "That's not my thing." CBS Sports reported Tatum's full comments Sunday night.

Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla was even more concise.

"It'll be fun," Mazzulla said. "It'll be a good atmosphere."

Brown is not the only centerpiece of the July deal who will face his former team.

George has settled quickly into Boston's lineup, averaging 20.4 points and supplying the high-volume outside shooting the Celtics have long prioritized. He scored 27 points and made five three-pointers Sunday as Boston beat Milwaukee for its third consecutive victory.

The Celtics have not needed George to duplicate everything Brown provided. He has fit alongside Tatum, Derrick White and Boston's returning core as another willing shooter and versatile defender.

Tatum is averaging 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists. His playmaking has been especially important for a team that replaced Brown's downhill pressure with more shooting and ball movement.

Boston enters Tuesday ranked third in offensive rating and fourth in defensive rating. It is one of two NBA teams currently inside the top five on both ends of the floor.

The Celtics have also made 15.6 three-pointers per game, the second-highest average in the league. They set an NBA Cup record by hitting 24 against Charlotte on Friday, then made 18 more Sunday in Milwaukee.

That presents a clear challenge for a Sixers defense that has generally performed well but has occasionally surrendered clean perimeter looks after committing extra help toward the ball. Tatum, George, White, Payton Pritchard and Sam Hauser can all punish late rotations.

The Sixers have reached 9-2 without depending upon the same formula every night.

Tyrese Maxey leads them at 26.9 points per game. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists while shooting 47.7 percent from the field and 39.2 percent from three. Joel Embiid and LeBron James have supplied scoring, passing and defensive flexibility around them.

Brown has repeatedly described the team as unfinished despite its record.

"From our perspective, it's been some growing pains for sure, even though we've been able to win," he said. "The result, we're not so much fixated on the result. It's more so about the process, and we've got to improve our process and our mentality to creating a winning environment."

Boston should provide the clearest early measure of that process.

The Celtics play considerably slower than the Sixers, but their half-court execution has been more efficient. Philadelphia will want to create turnovers and run before Boston can set its defense. The Celtics will attempt to control the pace, generate three-pointers and make the Sixers execute against a defense that has yet to allow an opposing player to score 30 points this season.

There is also the unavoidable Brown matchup. Boston could use Tatum, George and White against him at different points, giving the Celtics several defenders capable of absorbing his drives without immediately sending help.

Nick Nurse expects Brown to bring something extra, even if Brown has publicly downplayed the emotional component.

"It's going to be very different for him," Nurse said. "I think probably a little bit of emotion in there, too, but also I think he's going to be very motivated to play."

Boston's rotation is healthy entering the matchup. Two-way guard Devin Carter is out because of an illness.

Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti remain out for the Sixers. Adem Bona could return after missing Sunday's contest.

The betting market views the matchup as essentially a toss-up. Monday afternoon listings had the spread moving between Boston minus-1.5 and Philadelphia minus-1.5, depending on the sportsbook, with the total at 215.5.

That fits the larger picture. Philadelphia owns the East's best record. Boston has the conference's strongest point differential and has outscored opponents by 10.7 points per game.

The surrounding conversation will center on Brown and Tatum until the opening tip. Brown does not intend to contribute any ceremonial small talk.

"He's on his side," Brown said. "I'm on my side."

#2777. NHL Rumours: Philadelphia Flyers Forward Seeking Change of Scenery

Things are heating up in Philadelphia. The Philadelphia Flyers, amid their tumultuous start this season, may be facing more internal turmoil. Matvei Michkov has made it clear over the last week that he has been unhappy with his ice time with the Flyers. It should come as no surprise that NHL Rumours regarding the Flyers' leading goal scorer have surfaced.

Rumour: According to NHL analyst Kevin Weekes, Philadelphia Flyers forward Matvei Michkov is open to a change of scenery. Over the past week, Michkov has expressed discontent over his ice time, as Head Coach Rick Tocchet and Michkov have continued to have a difficult relationship. However, according to Emily Kaplan, Michkov has not formally requested a trade.

Analysis: This is a very intriguing rumour, as it expands the trade market, with the Dylan Larkin trade rumours and Nikita Kucherov trade request still active. Given that Michkov is wanting more ice time, this would be the best possible option for him.

To start this edition of NHL Rumours, let us go over Michkov's time with the Flyers. Over the past week, Michkov has talked to the media about his ice time."I want to play more," commented Michkov. "I like it all maximum, all shifts, all ice time, I want 60 minutes. I want lots of goals, lots of points." He leads the Flyers with ten goals and 14 points, but has only gotten an average of 15:54 of ice time per game.

Michkov's time with the Flyers has been a roller coaster. The seventh-overall pick in 2023 was seen by some as potentially the most talented player after Connor Bedard in his draft class. His contract with the KHL was a reason why some teams passed on him. However, Michkov was able to negotiate to be released from the KHL and joined Philadelphia for the 2024-25 season. His offensive production was prominent right away, as he scored 26 goals and 63 points in 80 games during his rookie year.

The defensive aspect of his game was a concern, but it was not until Rick Tocchet was hired that the problems started to surface. Michkov came to training camp out of shape, according to Tocchet. For Vancouver Canucks fans, this may sound eerily similar to how he dealt with Elias Pettersson, whose production also dipped during Tocchet's tenure. Sure, there may be truth to Tocchet's statements, but no doubt, it must have been frustrating from Michkov's perspective to see a reduction in ice time.

Michkov showed an improvement in his offseason preparation this season, but the team did not. Although Michkov's production has been solid, his ice time remains low, as Tocchet's deployment of young players remains a concern among both Michkov himself and the fans, who have voiced their displeasure over the deployment of young players through a fundraiser over the weekend. The fundraiser is looking to fund a banner reading "Fire Tocchet" that would fly over Xfinity Mobile Arena on November 27th, alongside a billboard near the arena.

Last night against the Vancouver Canucks, Michkov had a heated conversation with Nick Seeler over what could be Seeler's poor play. Porter Martone and Noel Acciari had to hold him back as Michkov's rage led him to throw a water bottle. Michkov's frustrations may have boiled over, because not only is he not getting the ice time he feels he deserves, but the team was also not playing the right way against the last-place Canucks.

It is clear that Michkov does not feel appreciated in Philadelphia, and a future with the team does not feel tenable. Given his offensive talent, many teams will be interested in the 21-year-old forward. No doubt, teams will be careful with Michkov's defensive inadequacies, but the offensive upside is still too good to pass up. Michkov is in the final season of his three-year entry-level contract and will be eligible for an offer sheet, so whichever team ends up taking Michkov will need to act relatively quickly in signing him to an extension.

#2776. With NFL's toughest schedule looming, Rams quiet at trade deadline as rivals make deals

High-profile trades before the season showed their fans and the rest of the NFL that with Super Bowl LXI to be played at SoFi Stadium, the Rams were unquestionably all in.

But as the league's trade deadline came and went Tuesday, the injury-ravaged Rams made only one minor move, essentially saying they'll handle this all internally.

While the NFC West-leading San Francisco 49ers added veteran receiver Keenan Allen, the Rams — with Davante Adams on injured reserve and Puka Nacua expected to be sidelined for an extended period — brought back receiver Xavier Smith, whom they released in October.

Read more: Rams star Puka Nacua likely will be placed on injured reserve

That is a far cry from moves the Rams made in previous Super Bowl seasons. In 2018, they traded for edge rusher Dante Fowler Jr. In 2021, they signed free-agent receiver Odell Beckham Jr. and traded for edge rusher Von Miller.

Coach Sean McVay indicated the last few weeks that the Rams were unlikely to be active at the deadline.

But that was before last Sunday, when Nacua suffered knee and toe injuries that are expected to sideline the All-Pro receiver for several weeks. The Rams were already thin at receiver after Adams suffered a hamstring injury that has kept him out of the lineup since Week 7.

"You have to look at all avenues to try to be able to solve some of the issues or situations or scenarios that have come up," McVay said Monday when asked if the Rams might pursue a receiver. "A lot of new things occur on a daily basis, so I would never rule it out."

Allen and Josh Downs of the Indianapolis Colts and Brian Thomas Jr. of the Jacksonville Jaguars were thought to be potential targets for the Rams.

Rams general manager Les Snead. (Kyusung Gong / Associated Press)

But the Jaguars ultimately took Thomas off the market. The 49ers, with receiver depth problems of their own, added Allen, and the Kansas City Chiefs traded for Downs.

The 49ers' move came after they had traded for defensive lineman DeForest Buckner ahead of the deadline. And the defending Super Bowl-champion Seattle Seahawks had bolstered their roster by trading for All-Pro offensive lineman Quenton Nelson.

Barring the Rams signing a free agent — the Minnesota Vikings released Beckham after the deadline and signed him to their practice squad — they will go into Sunday's game against the Arizona Cardinals with a receiver corps that includes Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, rookie CJ Daniels and Smith. The Rams re-signed Smith from the 49ers' practice squad after placing Jordan Whittington on injured reserve.

The Rams are 5-4 and have won three games in a row. But according to ESPN, they have the league's toughest remaining schedule.

Read more: 'I am that closer.' Myles Garrett's three-sack performance shows why Rams traded for him

After playing at the Cardinals, the Rams will have what is essentially a mini-bye before playing the Green Bay Packers at SoFi Stadium on the night before Thanksgiving.

Then they play the Chiefs, at the 49ers, the Dallas Cowboys and games against the Seahawks sandwiched around a game at Tampa Bay.

Defensive lineman Kobie Turner is expected to return against the Packers, and Adams, Nacua, tight end Terrance Ferguson and offensive lineman Steve Avila will be available at some point. But whether the Rams can remain in contention for a playoff spot is the all-encompassing question.

#2768. Payton Pritchard, Paul George preview highly anticipated Celtics-76ers matchup

The Celtics will face an old friend when they take on the 76ers on Tuesday night: Jaylen Brown, who spent a decade in Boston before being traded to Philadelphia on Tuesday.

And Payton Pritchard, one of Brown's longest-tenured teammates, looks forward to the match-up.

"I definitely had a lot of good memories with JB," he said in front of an unusually large media corp at the Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia. "Obviously, he was there from the moment I got drafted, and we had a good competitive battle. He pushed me to get better, so I'm definitely appreciative of that. And then, as far as tonight, two really great teams going at it, and there's nothing better than that."

Still, although there's heightened public interest in this match-up, the added emotions are nothing that he and the Celtics aren't used to.

"I've played a lot of playoff games, so I don't think it'll be that much different," Pritchard said. Three of those games came at the very arena where the Celtics held shootaround on Tuesday morning, just a few months ago, in the first round of the 2026 NBA Playoffs

Much of the discourse heading into Tuesday night will center on the dynamic between Brown and Jayson Tatum, whose relationship has been heavily scrutinized for years, especially in the last few weeks.

Paul George said he expects another big night from Tatum amid all the chaos.

"JT is locked in," George said. "He's as professional as they come at preparing for a game. He's been playing at an MVP level, and I think he's looking at it as another game on the schedule. Obviously, there's a lot of noise surrounding it that hopefully he's not lost in. But it's our job to support him, to help him do it, and make sure his focus is where it needs to be for us to come out here and have a chance to play against a really good team and continue to add to his MVP-performance resume this season."

Pritchard was asked at shootaround what people don't understand about NBA locker rooms, and how they differ from the locker rooms the general public is more familiar with, such as high school locker rooms.

"There's a lot of egos in it, and people need an ego to get to the NBA. And so it's definitely a balancing act," Pritchard said. "And in high school, like you said, it's all your buddies. Not to say that we're not all buddies, but everybody's got families. They're trying to make it. They got things to prove, so it's different. But in the day, I don't think there was ever beef or anything. I think it's working relationships. Some people are closer than others, but you find a way to win and keep going."

One storyline heading into Tuesday night is that Paul George will return to face the 76ers team he played for for two seasons. But there's not too much pressure on that return game for the 9-time All-Star.

"He said he's returned to four different teams before, so he's used to this," he said. "So it's nothing new to him."

George is averaging 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists, and 2.3 steals, while shooting 42.5% from three on the season.

"He's been unbelievable," Pritchard said. "He's played great to start the year and shooting the ball unbelievable. His defense is impeccable, so it's been huge for us."

George said at the Celtics shootaround that he's thoroughly enjoyed his tenure.

"I've been kind of blown away," he said. "I think it exceeded my expectations since being in Boston. #2767. NY Giants trade deadline analysis: Nothing happened, and that’s OK

The New York Giants tried to make a splash at the NFL trade deadline. They ended up not able to do anything.

Running back Jonathan Taylor was, of course, the player the Giants had targeted as a difference-maker for their offense — for this season and at least a couple of years to come. The Indianapolis Colts, though, chose to set a price tag no one, including the Giants, was willing to meet.

Multiple teams offered a second-round pick and more for Taylor. But the Colts wanted a blockbuster offer to even consider it. Instead, Taylor stays in Indy.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh said an hour before the deadline that he would be excited to have the "right player" join the team as it tries to win its first NFC East title since 2011.

"My excitement level would be based on who the player is," Harbaugh said. "You get the right player, then you're really excited."

Taylor could have been that guy. The price, though, was wrong.

"You don't want to make a bad deal. You make a bad deal, that doesn't make you better. That makes you worse," Harbaugh said. "Sometimes the best deal is a deal that you don't make.

"We're willing to pay a price to make our team better, but it's got to be something that really makes our team better, and it's got to be worth it."

On Monday, I asked Harbaugh about the idea of trying not to make an emotional decision at the trade deadline with the excitement of defeating the Philadelphia Eagles and leading the division being fresh.

Harbaugh said it was "very important" to take the emotion of the moment out of the decision-making process.

"You want to do everything you can do to make your team as strong as you can right now, because we're in the now, and we're told to live in the moment, be where our feet are planted, concern ourselves with today, but that's not at the expense of tomorrow or just prudent planning," Harbaugh said. "I think we just have to look at each situation, and just weigh it out in terms of, okay, what's the cost? What's the benefit? And is it worth it? Is it going to benefit us? Is it a good thing for the Giants, and for the organization, and the team?"

Taylor would have made the Giants stronger right now. The Giants, though, were correct to not overpay for a 27-year-old running back with high mileage. Just like they were correct a couple of years ago when they did not overpay in free agency for a 27-year-old running back with high mileage.

In the days leading up to the deadline, we watched the Jacksonville Jaguars make multiple trades — including outrageously giving the Philadelphia Eagles first- and second-round picks for defensive tackle Jordan Davis. We saw the Minnesota Vikings trade for quarterback Kirk Cousins. We saw the Buffalo Bills, San Francisco 49ers, and Kansas City Chiefs make "now" trades.

All of those teams have designs on winning a Super Bowl this season.

The Giants? They are not there yet. Winning the NFC East would be a massive accomplishment. Remember, they won seven games combined the last two seasons. It would be a tremendous step in the right direction for a proud franchise that has been down for most of the last 15 years.

I went on record a few days ago saying that I thought the Giants should make another run at Taylor, but that the price couldn't be more than the second-round pick plus that they had already offered.

Not giving away their first-round pick was the proper decision. In Harbaugh's words, the prudent one.

The Tennessee Titans did not want to trade running back Tony Pollard. He is a nice player, but Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy are nice players, too.

The Giants could have used defensive tackle help. They were never getting Jeffery Simmons, and they weren't foolish enough to give up a first-round pick for Davis. The Colts apparently wanted a fourth-round pick for Grover Stewart. The Giants didn't have one to give. They do have Malachi Fields. They didn't have a fifth-round pick. They do have J.J. McCarthy.

Harbaugh had warned on Sunday that the Giants would protect their future.

"We're not just going to go for a short term fix at an exorbitant cost," he said. "We're not going to do that. That's not where we're at."

Where they are at is leading the NFC East by 2.5 games. They have a 68.9% chance of winning the division, moves or no moves.

Getting Taylor, or another big-time difference-maker at the deadline would have been nice.

In the end, though, I think fans should be happy that Harbaugh and GM Joe Schoen kep their wits about them and protected the future.

The deadline end up to be boring for the Giants. Disappointing even, if you want to call it that. But, the Giants acted properly rather than desperately.

#2764. Kirk Cousins can become the first quarterback to play an 18-game regular season

With the Raiders trading him to the Vikings, Kirk Cousins has an opportunity to do something no quarterback has done before: Play 18 games in a single regular season.

Cousins has already started nine games this season for the Raiders, who have not had their bye. He’s now joining the Vikings, who have nine games left on their schedule because they have already had their bye. If Cousins plays every game the rest of the season, he’ll have played 18 regular-season games.

Since the NFL expanded the regular season to 17 games over 18 weeks in 2021, four players have played 18 games in a regular season because they moved from a team that hadn’t had its bye to a team that had: Rashid Shaheed and Dre’Mont Jones in 2025, Mike Williams in 2024 and Leonard Williams in 2023.

The NFL record for games in a season is actually 19, set by four members of the Frankford Yellow Jackets, a team that routinely played more games than other NFL teams in the 1920s. But in the modern era, 18 games has been the most a player could conceivably pay, and Cousins, as a starting quarterback, may become the most noteworthy player to do it.

#2763. 5 things Packers must do to win Super Bowl after quiet trade deadline

The trade deadline has come and gone without the Green Bay Packers making a significant move to upgrade the team, meaning their roster is pretty much set in stone for the rest of the season.

It was no surprise to see Brian Gutekunst stand pat, as there were very few options that actually made sense for Green Bay, especially if looking only at the players who were actually traded somewhere.

They were obviously not in a position to make big swings like the Bears and Jaguars did for Jeffery Simmons or Jordan Davis at defensive tackle, respectively, due to the hefty draft capital involved. DeForest Buckner could have been an option, but he only wanted to go to the 49ers.

Adding Quenton Nelson to the offensive line would have been nice. He was not cheap though and is a left guard only, with the right side more of the issue right now. Running backs Jonathan Taylor and Tony Pollard ended up not getting moved.

The Packers already made multiple signings on the offensive line in-season and Kevin Zeitler only saw his first snaps on Sunday. It is fair to let that situation play itself out as Green Bay keeps trying to figure out their 'best five' (more on that shortly).

With the roster unlikely to change much from here on out, and fresh off a dominant win in New England, here is what needs to happen for a Packers team that now looks like a real contender to win the Super Bowl:

Green Bay has already had its fill of devastating injuries to important players this season, with Zach Bako-Bewele, Jayden Reed, Edgerrin Cooper and Javon Hargrave all done for the year.

There are still eight regular seasons to go, and more injuries are bound to happen. The Packers cannot afford for any more of the season-ending variety to the caliber of players that have already been lost.

Jordan Love is 1A on that list, and this exceptionally explosive passing attack would also not be the same without either Christian Watson or Matthew Golden.

Tucker Kraft and arguably Jordan Morgan – who has really locked down the left side in pass protection lately – are also indispensable on offense given the lack of options behind them.

On defense, Jonathan Gannon has overcome some big losses, as well as the absence of Micah Parsons without skipping a beat, but there is only so much the group can take before the dam breaks.

They really only have two reliable three-down starters at defensive tackle in Devonte Wyatt and Karl Brooks, although they will hope to get Warren Brinson back from IR at some point.

The real engine of this defense is the secondary though, and if one of the tremendous trio of Evan Williams, Xavier McKinney or Javon Bullard went down, the knock-on effect on the entire unit could be massive.

Green Bay needs to pray to the injury gods that there are no more crushing blows on the horizon if this team is to go on a serious run.

More specifically, play Zeitler at right guard and Laken Tomlinson at left guard. PFF is certainly not gospel, but they gave Zeitler a 73.9 grade in his debut against the Patriots (in admittedly only 20 snaps), while Tomlinson has a 68.1 grade for the season.

Aaron Banks, who is still getting the red carpet treatment despite constantly being injured and not performing when he is in the lineup, has a 39.1 grade on the year.

The persistence with Banks, even forcing Tomlinson out of position to right guard to accommodate him, is likely due to his massive paycheck, and frankly that is not a good enough reason. It needs to stop, and it does seem like the tide is turning after Sunday's game.

Get Zeitler into the lineup, keep both him and Tomlinson at their natural spots and let the offensive line build chemistry. Once Sean Rhyan returns from injury, they may have a legitimately serviceable offensive line, which looked like a pipe dream two months ago.

There were also some green shoots in the run game against New England, as Green Bay managed four yards per carry as a team (the previous average was a paltry 2.85) and Kaleb Johnson had an encouraging day with a 4.9-yard average.

The Patriots are not usually easy to run against, and while the constant threat of the ball being thrown over their heads probably helped, that is an absolutely fine formula for the Packers to lean on moving forward, using the pass to set up the run, rather than the other way around.

If Green Bay can form some semblance of a viable run game by the time the playoffs arrive, centered around Johnson, Josh Jacobs and Karl Brooks, it will be a game changer for what has looked like one of the worst rushing attacks of all time for much of the year.

The wait to see Parsons back on the field has been longer than expected, so hopefully it will be worth it when he finally does suit up, which may come on Thanksgiving eve against the Rams.

Gannon has done a remarkable job with the defense, fashioning it into one of the league's best. A fit and firing Parsons could take them to a nuclear level.

While it will surely take him some time to get his feet back under him and look like his old self, Parsons needs to be at full power by the postseason to turn this into a true championship defense.

Sunday was a massive step forward for Smack after some real struggles of late. Relying on a rookie kicker is scary, as it can seem like they are rounding into form at times, before suffering another setback. Progression is not always linear.

That is the cost of doing business, but it can also cost you playoff games, as the Packers found out with Anders Carlson a few years back. By season's end, Green Bay must be in a position where they are able to trust Smack to deliver when it matters.

This article originally appeared on Packers Wire: 5 things Packers must do to win Super Bowl after quiet trade deadline

#2762. Tre Johnson is struggling from three. So are the Wizards

DETROIT — Tre Johnson is an elite shooter. It's why the Washington Wizards selected him No. 6 in the 2025 draft. But his jump shot hasn't clicked at the start of the 2026-27 season.

Johnson scored two points on 1-for-8 shooting in Monday's 122-111 loss to the Detroit Pistons just two days after shooting 2-for-15 in a 114-75 loss to the Oklahoma City Thunder. Johnson missed all 13 of his 3-point attempts in those contests.

He is shooting 35.1% from the field through 11 games. His 24.5% 3-point percentage is the second-worst in the NBA among players with at least 50 3-point attempts this season, trailing only Ace Bailey's 22.6%.

In Monday's loss, Johnson missed two wide-open triples — one in the far corner and another on the wing — in the first half. In the second half, he missed three more open looks to finish 0-for-6 from long range. His lone make was a 3-foot push shot that rimmed in.

Johnson is getting open looks. He's just missing them.

"[Johnson] had a great game in Atlanta the other night. This is what this guy does. I got great faith in him," Brian Keefe said. "He got some good looks tonight. He's gonna knock those down. We saw what he did last year with the percentage he shot. That'll turn. He puts in all the work, and I got great faith in him."

Johnson's struggles are concerning. But he's far from the only Wizards with an inefficient 3-ball. The Wizards made just nine of their 36 3-point attempts in Monday's loss. They're shooting 29% from three, which ranks 29th in the league.

Trae Young made just three of his 10 3-point attempts in Monday's loss. He's shooting 28.8% from three. Alex Sarr missed both of his outside jumpers to fall to 19.4% from three this season. Kyshawn George shot just 2-for-6 from long range.

Washington has a shooting problem. Keefe believes this slump will pass. But 11 games in, the Wizards' spacing concerns have been realized.

"We've got guys who can make them. I've got faith in our shooters. We're in a tough stretch shooting-wise, but these things will average out," Keefe said. " We're going to continue to do the right things, put ourselves in the position to make those shots, and I got faith in our guys."

AJ Dybantsa, who scored 21 points against Detroit but made just one of his four 3-point attempts, reiterated that sentiment. The rookie remained confident in the Wizards' ability to make open shots, especially from three.

"Keep shooting. We're NBA players. We're gonna knock shots down," Dybantsa said. "We might be in a shooting slump right now, but [we] have to keep shooting."

#2760. 2026 NFL trade deadline tracker: Grades, analysis and details from every key deal

The NFL trade deadline ended on Tuesday. We tracked every in-season deal and graded the key trades across the NFL.

Kirk Cousins to Vikings | Amani Hooker to Bills | Keenan Allen to 49ers | Jordan Davis to Jaguars | Jesse Bates to Jaguars | Jacoby Brissett to Ravens | Jeffery Simmons to Bears | Quenton Nelson to Seahawks | DeForest Buckner to 49ers | Marvin Harrison Jr. to Texans | Cam Jurgens to Ravens | Joey Porter to Cowboys | J.J. McCarthy to Giants | Broderick Jones to Cowboys

After Minnesota watched Carson Wentz flounder and realized Kyler Murray wouldn't be the answer, a bold move was needed at QB. Cousins has played pretty well this season, with 20 touchdowns and eight interceptions. He can come right in and run Kevin O'Connell's offense, which made him more valuable to Minnesota than some other teams.

The Raiders played the Kirk Cousins/Fernando Mendoza situation perfectly, as it turns out. They paid for half a season from Cousins and got a third-round pick out of it in the end. That's really smart business. Now is a good time to turn to rookie No. 1 pick Mendoza at QB anyway. — Frank Schwab

Buffalo acquiring a steady, productive, cost-controlled safety was a respectable move that filled a sizable hole on a defense that has given up a lot of big plays in the pass game. It's hard not to like the move, even at a moderately steep price.

For Tennessee, a second-round pick, even if it ends up being in the late 50s or 60s overall, is a darned good return for Hooker. It continues the team's process of offloading talent, following the deal that sent DT Jeffery Simmons to the Bears. — Eric Edholm

The 49ers got some help at receiver before the trade deadline without giving up too much. Allen isn't still the star he was with the Chargers earlier in his career, but he still knows how to get open and command targets. It's not a splashy move but it made complete sense.

That sixth-round pick is very unlikely to move the needle too much on what is going to be a long Colts rebuild, but it was fine value for a player the Colts had no more use for in a lost season. — Frank Schwab

The Jaguars left no doubt they're going for a Super Bowl this year by making their third trade of the day, following deals for Jessie Bates and Davon Godchaux. Davis was the biggest move of them all as Jacksonville paid a robust price for a big run-stopping tackle who can plug into the middle of the defense. The Eagles signed Davis to a three-year, $78 million extension in March, yet Davis' cap hit for 2027 is a very reasonable figure at just over $8.5 million.

For the Eagles, it's a tough short-term pill to swallow for the franchise and a fan base used to competing every season, but the long-term payoff could be immense. The Eagles' to-do list this offseason grows, but the potential of how they can reshape the roster is equally as exciting. — Eric Edholm

Safety flew beneath the radar a bit for Jacksonville, but injuries made it a position of some concern. Bates has a lot of qualities that fit the Jaguars seek. He's one of the league's better center fielders — and he's a ballhawk. It comes at a cost, however. Bates is set to hit free agency, and given the team's tight cap situation, he could end up being a half-season rental.

Bates is the ideal type of asset to trade off in this situation, given his expiring contract and reaching a point in his career where his value might start to depreciate. Getting back a plum draft pick for an expiring contract made it well worth the price. — Eric Edholm

Nobody should believe Brissett will save Baltimore's season and help it win a division. But he was the best option available, and he at least makes sure the Ravens aren't playing out the string with uncompetitive football for two months. And maybe a miracle happens and the Ravens are still in contention by the time Lamar Jackson returns, if he can this season.

It's a reasonable move for the Cardinals, who are going to start rookie Carson Beck soon to get a look at him by next season. Gardner Minshew can do as well as Brissett in the short term. They get to add draft capital for a player who wasn't going to see the field the rest of the season and has an expiring contract. — Frank Schwab

Value-wise, this is close to as much compensation as you'll see moved for a defensive player. But if the Bears make a Super Bowl run, the price very well could make the move a smart one. This trade sends a clear signal that the Bears are going for it all this season.

The Titans are facing a multi-year rebuild, and this was the best way to help starting toward that effort. They have more needs today than they did yesterday, and picks are merely lottery tickets, but this felt like a deal GM Mike Borgonzi had to make. – Eric Edholm

The Colts have other players who are far less tethered to the organization who also soon could be moved. Lacking a first-round draft pick next year from the Sauce Gardner trade, the Colts are trying to recoup as much draft-pick value as possible before the spring. With Daniel Jones' struggles, along with the Colts' apparent lack of trust in Anthony Richardson Sr., the team almost certainly will be going QB hunting in the offseason. …

Given the stage of his career and his contract status, this could end up being a fairly pricy rental for the Seahawks — and that potential cost must be baked into the team's grade. But if Nelson plays to his expected level, or even above the level he's played at this season, and the Seahawks remain a title contender, it would be hard to label this as anything but a win. – Eric Edholm

The 49ers needed defensive help up front, and Buckner looks like the right-shaped peg for their hole inside. Osa Odighizuwa has supplied some pressure, and rookie Gracen Halton has had some big moments, but they're the only Niners DTs to play every game. There weren't many other dependable pieces inside. The Colts got about what could be expected in return, and considering how depleted their draft-pick drawer is with no first-round pick next year, every pick counts. Even with the 2027 selections they got for Nelson and Buckner likely falling closer to the ends of those respective rounds, the Colts are accumulating more immediate assets to compete for a quarterback next year. It was reported Oct. 10 that the Cardinals were finalizing details on a trade for Harrison, but no team was announced. CINCINNATI (AP) — The Cincinnati Bengals backed out of a trade for Philadelphia Eagles edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie because it would have resulted in the loss of a third-round compensatory pick in the 2027 NFL draft.

The potential roadblock was first unearthed on social media by Over the Cap's Nick Korte after NFL Network reported the trade was in the works.

#2757. 30 Fantasy Basketball Takes on Every NBA Team: The rookie takeover is changing rotations

Here are five fantasy trends grabbing my attention heading into Week 4 of the fantasy basketball season, plus some rapid-fire notes on every other team.

Heat: One of the bigger surprises has been Miami's Davion Mitchell, who's ranked inside the top 55 in both 9-cat and standard points leagues, outpacing his ADP of 118.7. Warriors: F Yaxel Lendeborg is another draft-day bargain, ranking 54th in 9-cat and 37th in points leagues after carrying an ADP of 104. His usage ranks fourth, but he has the highest TS% among rookies playing at least 20 minutes a night. The efficiency at high-end minutes (32.3 per game) with a defined role led to some nice cross-category value across scoring, rebounding, facilitating and defensive production. I'm buying the breakout and hard-pressed to find a reason to sell. He's that good.

Clippers: LAC is hoarding one of the best fantasy values in Kris Dunn. He's sitting at 33rd in 9-cat, despite being drafted in the late rounds (ADP 119). The steals he's piling up (over 2 per contest) are what's driving most of his rise up the ranks. He's playing a ton of minutes while keeping his turnovers down and delivering a versatile 9-4-4 line with almost 3 steals a night. There's some sell-high appeal here, especially in 9-cat leagues. In 42% of Dunn trades, he's part of a package deal, so you'll likely have to include someone else to make a swap.

Timberwolves: Let's not gloss over Minnesota's Jaden McDaniels, who is crushing his ADP (ranked 46th in 9-cat after going 89th on draft day). Through 11 games, he's on pace for career-bests in minutes, points, rebounds, assists, 3s and usage per game. I think his defense will pick up once Ant-Man returns and he carries less responsibility on the offensive end.

Kings: Sacramento's Darius Acuff Jr. has a crazy high 32.3% usage rate, eighth in the NBA among qualified players. That's a massive offensive responsibility for a rookie, and the Kings' 1-9 start gives them little reason to limit his development. His scoring (25.9 ppg) and assists (7.4 apg) make him especially appealing in points leagues. Although, even with his warts in inefficiency and turnovers, he's in the top 80 in 9-cat, well above his preseason ADP.

Bucks: In Milwaukee, Brayden Burries has overtaken Ryan Rollins in the starting lineup. Burries is averaging 13 points, 8.3 rebounds and 3.5 assists across three starts. #2751. Tale of the tape: Bills were able to find solutions to Vikings blitz as game progressed

The Buffalo Bills learned firsthand that more blockers doesn't guarantee better protection.

The Minnesota Vikings defense entered the game blitzing an NFL-high 71% of the time, more than double the league average. And the Bills came out with a game plan that respected the blitz and the chaos it created.

Throughout much of the first half, the NFL's top-ranked scoring defense outdueled the league's top scoring offense. A combination of miscommunication on the offensive line — which was without left tackle Dion Dawkins (rib) and left guard Alec Anderson (ankle) — a glitch in the game plan and quarterback Josh Allen playing hurriedly caused the passing game to sputter.

But the Bills gradually started to find a rhythm and produced a big scoring drive that ended with an Allen-to-Keleki Latu 25-yard touchdown pass before halftime in a 23-6 win.

Allen went 6 of 11 for 44 yards, an interception and three sacks against the Minnesota blitz during the first half, but turned it around in the second half to go 6 of 9 for 64 yards and a sack when the Vikings sent five or more rushers.

One way the Bills sparked their passing game was by stepping away from heavy protection schemes. Having more blockers may seem like a grand idea to protect Allen, but it actually was what the Vikings wanted them to do.

Minnesota tricks opponents into locking in their protection rules before sending unblocked pressure from unexpected angles. Even if there are more blockers than rushers, it's hard to shift once the protection is set.

And if the offense commits six (or more) blockers for five rushers, the Vikings have more defenders than the offense has receivers in the pattern. Bills coach Joe Brady only sent five receivers out 10 times in the game against the blitz, but they were effective.

With six or more blockers, Allen went 4 of 12 for 40 yards, with an interception and two sacks. On plays with just five blockers, Allen went 8 of 8 for 71 yards and two sacks.

On first down from their own 15-yard line in the second quarter, the Bills tried to run a play-action pass. The protection was faulty, as a miscommunication between left guard Austin Corbett and left tackle Tylan Grable allowed Minnesota defensive tackle Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins to split them.

But the bigger problem was that the Bills only had two receivers in the pattern — both beyond the sticks — and the Vikings had five in coverage. Had a check-down or underneath option been available, Allen could have released the ball quickly to avoid being sacked.

"I don't think we were (efficient on first down) in the first half," Allen said. "In the second half, I thought we wore down on them and skipped some third downs. … Second and long, they're getting to their third down menu, they're making it really tough for opposing offenses. The best way out of that is stay out of second-and-long, third-and-long situations."

With 4:04 left in the third quarter, the Bills got a first down at their own 39 and once again went with a play-action pass. The Vikings only sent five, but the Bills only used five to block them.

The protection was more in sync, with a nifty wrinkle that saw Corbett pull to the right edge and block outside linebacker Kyle Van Noy. And while the Vikings still had a one-man advantage in the secondary, spacing gave Allen multiple options.

Allen could have hit D.J. Moore in the right flat or Ray Davis in the left flat. He also had tight end Dawson Knox over the middle. Throws to Moore and Knox likely would have netted a first down, but Allen also had Khalil Shakir running open 10 yards behind Knox and he delivered it for an easy 22-yard gain.

In a clash between high-powered offense and elite defense, patience ultimately determined the winner — and the Bills outlasted Minnesota.

#2749. The Kirk Cousins contract points to a revised deal or termination after 2026

The last time the Vikings brought back a key former player for a third-round pick, the reunion didn’t last long. This time, it will last longer — but possibly not beyond the current season.

In 2010, the Vikings sent a third-round pick to the Patriots for receiver Randy Moss, whom the Vikings had traded to the Raiders in 2005. Former coach Brad Childress, calling Moss a “programmatic non-fit,” released Moss after four games.

Now, quarterback Kirk Cousins returns for a third-round pick, and a contract that covers nine regular-season games. His deal with the Raiders was structured to maximize the amount the Falcons owed Cousins for 2026 ($8.7 million, on top of the $90 million he made in 2024 and 2025) with another $10 million paid by the Raiders to Cousins in 2027, in the form of a guaranteed roster bonus not subject to offset.

The contract also includes a 2028 base salary of $78.655 million that becomes fully guaranteed on the fifth day of the 2027 league year. Coupled with a $1.345 million base salary in 2027 that becomes fully guaranteed that same day, the Vikings would be on the hook for $80 million over two years if he’s not released by then.

Without a revised deal, the current contract surely would be torn up by March. The question is whether the Vikings and Cousins would be able to come up with a new contract to replace it.

Much of that depends on how the rest of the year goes. Still, Cousins has the ability to force his way to free agency, for the fourth time in his career, by simply declining to re-do the existing deal.

However it plays out, Cousins can be counted on to make a good business decision. He has $333 million in career earnings, which has him at fourth on the all-time list.

On-field success is a different story. He has made it to the postseason three times in his career, with one playoff win.

If, as expected, the return of Cousins provides a B-12 shot to the Minnesota franchise, he has a realistic chance of getting back to the playoffs. And of winning a second postseason game.

And maybe a third. Hell, maybe even a fourth.
