#2747. The top 5 biggest impact deadline trades, including Jaguars and Bears shooting for a Super Bowl

The NFL trade deadline had plenty of action.

There were multiple teams who traded for a new starting quarterback. Stars at all three levels of the defense were dealt. There were well-known offensive linemen and receivers moved. Strangely, after weeks of chatter, the only position that didn't see a trade was running back. But there were enough deals to keep everyone busy.

Here are the five most impactful trades made since the start of this season:

Simmons showed in his first game at Seattle how much he will impact the Bears this season. The Chicago defense looked much different with Simmons in the middle, taking up attention from blockers and still making plays. He was a first-team All-Pro last season and could be on a similar path this season. Everyone had seen how dominant Simmons was, the Bears were just the team that acted on it. They sent two first-round picks to Tennessee for Simmons, who is 29 years old, but the Bears and their fans won't mind if he helps break a Super Bowl drought that dates back to the 1985 season. Given how good Chicago's offense is and how the defense has improved already with Simmons in the middle, it's realistic to think Chicago could find itself in the Super Bowl.

"I think he's just — I don't know — you can feel his presence," linebacker T.J. Edwards said after Simmons' Week 8 Bears debut, according to the team's site. "Especially me, I'm right behind him, so I can kind of just feel how they're trying to block him. I feel like [the defense] was just flying today. They made our job a whole lot easier. But he definitely helps, for sure."

The Eagles had a lot of potential trade chips, but Davis wasn't discussed as one because he was just 26 years old and also one of the highest paid defensive tackles in the NFL. But the Jaguars got aggressive, sending a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick to the Eagles for a player who immediately can replace (and potentially upgrade) from DaVon Hamilton, who was having a tremendous season before he tore his quadriceps and went to injured reserve. It was a very expensive trade, and probably an overpay, but Davis unquestionably makes the Jaguars stronger this season.

The Jaguars also made moves for safety Jessie Bates III and another defensive tackle, Davon Godchaux, but the move for Davis is the big difference-maker for a team that clearly has Super Bowl hopes.

We have to be careful to not overrate the impact of this move. The Vikings still have the fourth-best quarterback and fourth-best offense in their own division. Cousins is 38 years old. And many of the same people who were clamoring for the Vikings to trade for Cousins were the same ones that, during Cousins' previous six seasons in Minnesota, said he could never win anything.

But, it's the kind of move that is very rare in the NFL. Viable starting quarterbacks are rarely available in a trade. The Vikings didn't pay too much, a third-round pick, and it's the rare situation of a quarterback who has played with the coach and in the scheme before. He can step right in. The Vikings have a fantastic defense and now should have a competent offense. Wherever this reunion leads, it was smart for the Vikings to find out.

Hooker is having a career year in his eighth season. He leads the NFL with five interceptions. His Pro Football Focus grade ranks fourth among all NFL safeties with at least 300 snaps. The Bills had a hole at safety after cutting C. J. Gardner-Johnson and did well to land Hooker.

The Bills' defense started slow this season and while it has played well for two weeks, that came against quarterbacks Joe Fagnano and Carson Wentz. Buffalo needed an upgrade on defense. The Bills are pretty good up front, and now they have a potential All-Pro safety this season for the back end. It was a sharp move that should improve the Bills, who are in a great spot to make the Super Bowl for the first time in the Josh Allen era.

When the Giants traded a fifth-round pick for McCarthy, it seemed like a low-cost gamble on a reclamation project. The Giants couldn't have known they had found a starting quarterback for a team that is still in first place of the NFC East. McCarthy had a blistering fourth quarter in relief of Jameis Winston against the Saints, throwing for 243 yards in less than a quarter. He got the starting job after that and the Giants have won both games since.

It's possible McCarthy reverts to the inconsistent form he had last season, which caused the Vikings to give up on the 10th overall pick of the 2024 NFL Draft after only 10 starts. But he has looked poised and gives the Giants a more stable option at quarterback than the hot-and-cold Winston. It seemed like the GIants' season might have been done when Jaxson Dart suffered a knee injury in Week 2, but a smart and cheap trade for McCarthy could end up saving it.

#2737. Steve Kerr sounds alarm over Warriors’ latest injury: ‘It’s a big concern’

The Golden State Warriors have won eight straight games and look like one of the Western Conference's best teams.

But it was not all smiles for Golden State after Monday's 138-87 win over the New Orleans Pelicans, given the injury that backup point guard Brandon Williams suffered.

Warriors head coach Steve Kerr spoke about how much of a blow Williams' injury is when speaking to the media postgame.

Golden State Warriors head coach Steve Kerr speaks to the media during a pregame press conference before a game against the Miami Heat, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Yalonda M. James/San Francisco Chronicle via AP

"Yeah, it's a big concern. He's a huge part of our team, and he's given us such a lift. And it's a hamstring. He's going to get an MRI, so we'll see how bad it is," Kerr said on Williams' injury.

Williams has been one of the Warriors' best surprises this season. He is averaging 10.4 points in 16.1 minutes per game for Golden State after signing a one-year, $2.6 million for them this past offseason.

Brandon Williams of the Golden State Warriors handles the ball against the Orlando Magic at Chase Center in San Francisco, California, Nov. 7, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Brandon Williams (12) of the Golden State Warriors shoots a free throw against the Orlando Magic at Chase Center in San Francisco on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

#2729. Bills offense dominates time of possession, grinds down valiant Vikings defense

Joe Brady likes to say the Buffalo Bills play nameless, faceless opponents.

The Minnesota Vikings can probably say the same, but only because they bring enough heat to peel the faces off opposing offenses, bolstering a high-blitzing phisolsophy by being fast, physical and intelligent.

When someone looks at the statistics down the road, they might think the Bills had an off game. They had season-lows in points (23), total yards (339) and yards per play (4.3) And yet the Vikings allowed season-high 23 points in a 23-6 loss.

There have been times Josh Allen and the Bills have grown frustrated playing small ball, leaning on the run game and resisting the urge to hunt splash plays. Not against the Vikings. They won ugly; they grinded out the win.

The Vikings had only allowed one 80-yard drive all season — a one-play, 81-yard drive against the Green Bay Packers in the first quarter of the season opener — and the Bills produced three, choking out Minnesota by holding the ball over 42 minutes.

"Time of possession is good. Yards is good. It's only good if you're scoring touchdowns," Brady said. "... The guys stuck together and found a way to win. They earned that win. Finding a way is the wrong term, but they earned it."

Typically Josh Allen draws special game plans. Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores just did what he does to everyone: blitz.

The Vikings, who blitz 71% of the time — almost 40 points higher than the league average and 30 points more than the next highest defense — send five or more rushers on 12 of Allen's first 15 drop-backs. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, they blitzed him on 68% of his 35 drop-backs and it was ugly for most of the first half.

The Bills attempted to counter Minnesota's blitz by using six or seven players in pass protection. They had five players run routes just 10 times, the lowest rate of Brady's career as a play-caller. And, at times, it was counterproductive.

While the Vikings sometimes walk eight players to the line of scrimmage, they are most often only sending five. So when the Bills ran three-man routes, they had six players in coverage. Combine that with the Bills struggling to find which five were rushing and Allen was sacked four times, including three in the first half.

Allen started the game 6 of 14 for 52 yards, with a sack squandering a 58-yard game-opening kick return by Greg Dortch and an interception nullifying a second drive, as the Bills got just three points despite having the ball inside the Minnesota 40 on three straight drives to start the game.

But after three previous drives netted a total of minus-3 yards on 11 plays, the Bills got the ball with 4:02 left in the first half. Brady went to the quick passing game and immediately found success, going 80 yards on eight plays.

Allen got into a rhythm, going 6 of 6 for 70 yards. The Vikings finally chose not to blitz and Allen was able to extend the play to find tight end Keleki Latu in the end zone for his first career touchdown catch to take a 10-3 lead.

From that drive, Allen went 15 of 17 for 182 yards, finishing with 234 for the game, which is the most allowed by the Vikings since Green Bay's Jordan Love threw for 387 in Week 1.

"Those guys are coming, they're coming fast," Allen said. "They're so smart on the back end. They're able to read and flow with eyes. … That's a tough defense."

But Brady had decided leading up to the game that the best way to beat the Vikings was to wear them down. He watched the Detroit Lions run for 230 yards and hold the ball for nearly 36 minutes, something he referenced earlier in the week.

It became even more appealing when they ruled out left tackle Dion Dawkins (rib) and left guard Alec Anderson (ankle) before the game. That moved veteran Austin Corbett into the lineup at left guard and Tylan Grable — who made his NFL first start last week at right tackle for Spencer Brown — to left tackle.

Cook didn't have much room to run, totaling just 18 yards on his first 10 carries. In fact, Cook had one run over 10 yards the entire game and it came in the fourth quarter, one play before Cook sealed the game with a 5-yard touchdown run to take a 20-6 lead.

The Bills gobbled 8:32 off the clock and used 15 plays to march 84 yards on that drive, with Cook carrying eight times for 45 yards. He finished with 107 yards on 31 attempts.

It's one thing for an offense to score points — and no team scores more than the Bills — but it's another to use an offense to control the game simply by managing the clock and controlling the tempo.

"Eventually you end up making it a game that they weren't willing to play," Brady said. "That's a good football team and that's a great defense. And to be able to just stay on the field and be able to possess the ball, is really hard. … Really proud of that locker room."

#2727. Lakers ‘registered interest’ in Nique Clifford before trade to Thunder

On Sunday afternoon, the Sacramento Kings agreed to deal second-year wing Nique Clifford to the Oklahoma City Thunder in exchange for two second-round picks. Clifford held a fairly sizable role during his rookie season, when he averaged 8.6 points, 3.8 rebounds, 2.4 assists and 0.9 steals in 25.1 minutes per game.

But he'd fallen out of Sacramento's rotation to begin 2026-27 and played just 50 minutes in eight games prior to the trade. With the Thunder ravaged by early season injuries, they opted to tap into their surplus of picks and add a reinforcement to their wing room with the hopes he might break out in a more stable organization.

Oklahoma City, however, was not the lone playoff hopeful eyeing Clifford. Marc Stein and Jake Fischer reported that a trio of other suitors, including the Los Angeles Lakers, gauged the market for him. Ultimately, though, the Thunder emerged victorious in the Nique Clifford Sweepstakes.

"The Pacers, Nuggets and Lakers, sources say, were among the teams that registered trade interest in the 24-year-old," according to The Stein Line Substack, "but Oklahoma City had multiple advantages when it came to getting a deal done."

Among the "multiple advantages" referenced there is presumably Oklahoma City's wealth of picks. Between 2027 and 2033, it owns 15 second-round picks, one of which is Los Angeles' 2032 second-rounder. For comparison, the Lakers own just three over that same span.

Plus, the Lakers are also already fairly well-stocked with youthful wings worth taking a swing on this season. Adou Thiero (22 years old), Cameron Carr (22) and Ziaire Williams (25) are all 25 or younger and have garnered varying levels of rotation minutes to open the year. Given the Lakers' depleted well of draft capital, it probably didn't make much sense to fork over two of their remaining three second-round picks through 2033 for a dude who *might* crack the rotation on certain nights.

If they're going to move some of those picks, it should be for someone they know can be a difference-maker and mainstay in the rotation. Clifford, while still pretty young and far from a finished product in the league, certainly does not fit that billing.

#2722. ‘There’s lots of things about that program that are fantastic’: Arizona coach Brent Brennan previews big-time matchup vs. Utah

Arizona is preparing for its biggest game of the season, and coach Brent Brennan wants to see a full house.

The Wildcats have yet to sell out the 50,782-seat Casino Del Sol Stadium this season, and haven't sold out the stadium since a 2024 game against Colorado, per Tucson.com writer Justin Spears.

With No. 3 Utah in town, Fox pregame show Big Noon Kickoff broadcasting live from Tucson and a 5:30 p.m. MST kickoff, Brennan is ready to see Tucson show up to support the No. 22 Wildcats.

"This is the game to show up for your alma mater, to show up for your university or show up for this city and how this institution is wired into the city of Tucson," Brennan said at his weekly press conference.

"... Let's show everybody how freaking dope the city of Tucson is. Let's show them what this institution, the University of Arizona, is all about by going absolutely nuts."

Brennan pointed to the atmosphere at Rice-Eccles Stadium in Utah's 28-20 win over BYU as a bit of inspiration for the Arizona home crowd.

"It looked fantastic. Yeah, it looked great. I've coached in a bunch of games there over the course of my career as an assistant and as a head coach and they have a great game day," Brennan said. "You could see that it had an impact on BYU at times in that game, and that's what I'm talking about here in Casino Del Sol Stadium on Saturday night. Our fan base, the Zona Zoo, our alums, the city making that incredibly challenging for Utah."

The stakes are especially high for Arizona, which is 4-2 in Big 12 play. The Wildcats need an upset win over the undefeated Utes to remain in the Big 12 title race and have a still have a chance at making the College Football Playoff.

For Utah, a victory not only preserves an undefeated season, but moves the Utes one win away from clinching their first-ever spot in the Big 12 championship game in the event's final year of operation.

Whether the atmosphere turns out to be formidable or not, the Utes are facing a formidable opponent in Arizona. Add in the fact that the Utes have to hit the road following an emotional rivalry win over No. 9 BYU last week, and it's going to require everything Utah has to come out of Tucson with a win.

Quarterback Noah Fifita has had Utah's number in the last two meetings — a 42-18 loss that was the low point of the Utes' 2023 season and a 23-10 loss in 2024. Utah's defense will be tested once again by a fast-paced, explosive offense led by a good quarterback.

Fifita is fourth in the nation in passing yards this season (2,794) and has one of the nation's highest explosive pass percentages (7.8% of his pass plays result in a gain of 30 or more yards, per Hudl IQ).

Utah has given up explosive passing plays in nearly every Big 12 game, and has allowed 233.8 passing yards per game, ranking No. 102 in FBS. Yet it's tough to bet against the Utes' defense after what they've shown through the first nine games, including wins against top-15 opponents BYU and Houston.

Utah's red-zone defense has been stellar, and despite giving up a lot of passing yards, the Utes rank No. 15 in the nation in points per game with 16.3. Utah has also intercepted opposing quarterbacks 13 times, tied for No. 4 in the country.

"They're super good on defense, incredibly good in the red zone. And so it's going to be a physical, physical game and that's what it is every time you play Utah," Brennan said.

Quarterback Devon Dampier and Utah's offense, however, dominated the talk in Brennan's press conference.

Dampier registered four touchdowns in Utah's win over BYU, two of which were rushing scores. The dual-threat senior presents a big challenge for Arizona's defense.

"That's kryptonite in all of football. Who are the best quarterbacks in the NFL? All the guys that can move. So guys that they're able to utilize plus-one run game or escape these incredibly athletic, twitchy defensive linemen," Brennan said.

"So I think that's a challenge for all of college football and obviously Dampier is exceptional at it."

Arizona will hope to contain Dampier's rushing abilities, but Brennan is not tipping his game plan, obviously.

"We're getting ready to play the No. 2 team in the country. I'm not going to give you anything schematically or how are we going to slow down this incredible player, right?" Brennan said. "But we're going to do everything we can to do it. And they combine that with a great running game. They got receivers that can make plays. They got a bunch of big tight ends. Their O-line is massive and athletic and tough."

Brennan is familiar with Utah's offensive brain trust in offensive coordinator Kevin McGiven and quarterbacks coach Ryan Gunderson, working with the pair at both Oregon State and San Jose State. He also worked with Utah safeties coach Derrick Odum at San Jose State.

"Those guys are really good people and really good football coaches. The success they're having doesn't surprise me because I believe in those guys," Brennan said.

Brennan has coached against Scalley as a defensive coordinator a number of times, both as a head coach and assistant coach, but Saturday will be the first time facing off against Scalley as a head coach.

Brennan has a lot of respect for Utah's program heading into Saturday night's big-time matchup.

"There's lots of things about that program that are fantastic. There's been a consistency there. They've played in the Rose Bowl. They've won the conference. I know it was the old conference (Pac-12), but they've done a great job since moving from the Mountain West into the Power Four," Brennan said.

"I got a ton of respect for what they do there. Coach Scalley's doing a great job. They're very well-coached. Three guys that I worked with over the course of my career are coaching on that staff there. I love those guys. I believe in them. I'm happy for them and I'm excited for this big-time matchup on Saturday night."

#2720. Paul George treating return to Philly as “a regular game”

Lost in the background of the highly anticipated first matchup between Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum is a return to Philadelphia for Paul George, who spent his past two seasons as a Sixer.

Both Brown and Tatum have downplayed the narrative, as hard as it is to ignore. George, who played 89 games in a Sixers uniform, is following suit.

"It's a regular game — that's how I'm treating it," he said during Boston's morning shootaround.

George said he was unsure of the reception he'd receive in his first game back to Xfinity Mobile Arena, a place where in his last appearance, he scored a series-best 23 points on 47% efficiency to go with vintage defense, forcing four Celtics turnovers and holding shooters matched up with him to 33% (5/15 FG). It played a part in Philly completing the 14th 3-1 series comeback in NBA history.

And yet, George's brief stint in Philadelphia was defined by a core group that struggled to stay on the floor at the same time, and ran into the same second round demons they've yet to exorcise since the beginning of The Process.

"Had I been here 8, 9, 10 years it'd be a different story. I was there 2 years," he said.

It's an easy narrative to shrug off for George because, over his 17 seasons, he's gone through this same thing before.

"He said he's returned to four different teams before. There's nothing new to him," Payton Pritchard said.

George had his own contentious reunion when he played against the Indiana Pacers for the first time, followed by games against the Thunder and Clippers.

George isn't the only Celtic currently on the roster to have experienced an anticipated reunion between a foundational player and the team that drafted him.

Mike Conley, a 12-year Grizzlies mainstay before the organization ended the Grit and Grind with a full scale rebuild, was showered with appreciation and given a hero's welcome from the Memphis fanbase in his first game against them in 2019.

Their experiences couldn't have been farther apart.

In the case of George, whose seven years in Indiana ended in a trade request, he first played the Pacers in Oklahoma City, struggling with foul trouble and playing just 19 minutes in an 18-point win. When he played in Indiana for the first time later that season, he was showered with boos from the moment his name was announced, and he shot just 3-of-14 for 12 points, though a late steal and two clutch free throws contributed to a 100-95 win.

"I'm happy this circus is over with. Everybody can move on," George said after his return to Indiana.

The response was different in George's next stop; he was given a tribute video and crowd ovation playing against the Thunder for the first time. Against the Clippers, a video tribute was also presented, but there was a mix of cheers and boos, a reaction he described as "stupid," though he cited no ill will towards the franchise or his time spent in Los Angeles.

"The boos, I didn't get it," he said after his first game against the Clippers. "I still don't get it when I go [back] to Indy, but it is what it is. It's sports. I look forward to next year being back here and more boos."

It's hard to say the exact response when George's name is called in the lineup introductions tonight. As the Celtics got rolling on their shootaround inside Xfinity Mobile Arena, the song "Why Can't We Be Friends" by War blared from the speakers, a tongue and cheek choice to kick off what will be one of the most watched and debated rivalry games of the season.

Perhaps it's a sign that tempers will be calm on Tuesday night. The game will be played, hands will be shaken, and hugs will be dispersed from competitor to competitor after an early November test between two Eastern Conference contenders.

The NFL trade deadline is at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10, and PFT has you covered with news and analysis of every trade, potential trade, rumor of a trade and trade that won’t be happening.

Kirk Cousins to Vikings: Cousins is returning to Minnesota, while the Vikings are sending a 2027 third-round pick to Las Vegas.

Colts may trade more players: Indianapolis has told teams it wants more than a fourth-round pick for Josh Downs. Jonathan Taylor and Daniel Jones could both be traded, perhaps both to the Vikings.

Jacoby Brissett is headed to Baltimore: The Ravens and Cardinals announced a deal sending the veteran quarterback and a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Ravens for a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 seventh-round pick.

Derrick Henry says he’s not thinking about changing teams: The Ravens star expressed a desire to help the team improve after a fourth-straight loss.

Jonathan Taylor wants to know where he’ll finish the season: Taylor said no one likes uncertainty when asked about talk that the Colts will trade him.

Chargers say they’re not trading Khalil Mack: Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh said, “I want Khalil Mack to be here and Khalil Mack wants to be here.”

#2716. Falcons steal K Jake Moody from Ravens’ practice squad

The Baltimore Ravens need a new kicker. Again.

The Atlanta Falcons are signing Jake Moody off of the Ravens' practice squad, per NFL insider Jordan Schultz, robbing Baltimore of another kicker less than a week after Week 1 starter Tyler Loop landed on injured reserve with a groin injury.

The move raises questions about the Ravens' approach to their kicker situation with Loop sidelined for at least four games. The team had a roster spot available, but opted to elevate Moody from the practice squad to face the Jacksonville Jaguars last Thursday. With only two elevations remaining, he would have required a promotion to the 53-man roster to see out Loop's absence, which would have also precluded his departure to Atlanta. Logic suggests that the Ravens should have just promoted Moody knowing they would need him to kick for the rest of the month, maybe longer.

Additional reporting from Jeff Zrebiec of The Athletic indicated that the Ravens were "willing" to promote Moody to their active roster on Monday. The Falcons, though, offered a better situation after releasing kicker Jason Sanders: a potential long-term job for Moody and a home field enclosed by a dome.

It still seems, though, that Baltimore could have headed off this entire issue had they promoted Moody to the active roster last week. It is possible that his agent was keeping tabs on the Falcons' kicking situation and preferred a practice squad stay to preserve his options. However, Loop has not exactly inspired much confidence that he can deliver key kicks for a team that will need to win at the margins to make the playoffs this year. There is an argument that the Ravens should have identified Moody as their kicker for the foreseeable future and adjusted their roster accordingly.

Instead, they will have to scour the NFL's practice squads and free-agent pool to find their next kicker. Signing Nick Folk, who the Falcons cut to add Moody, would be an ironic twist. After three straight years of leading the league with a field goal conversion rate of 95.5% or better, the 42-year-old's numbers have collapsed in 2026. He made just 72.2% of his field goals to start the season with two misses inside of 50 yards and a one-for-four mark from beyond.

#2710. Jamie Little Stepping Away From The Booth, Will Focus on Pit Road Duties in 2027

FOX NASCAR reporter Jamie Little announced on Tuesday that she will shift her focus away from play-by-play commentary beginning next year. Little intends to prioritize her role as a NASCAR on FOX pit reporter in the Cup Series, as well as select IndyCar Series races.

For the last six years, Little has expanded her role at FOX as the lead play-by-play announcer for the Craftsman Truck Series and the ARCA Menards Series. FS1, the FOX sports channel owned by the FOX corporation, is the exclusive home of both the Truck Series and ARCA Menards Series.

Little has been a pit reporter for NASCAR since 2007 for a number of different networks, including ABC, ESPN, and FOX.

On social media, Little put out a post making her intentions known for 2027. The pit reporter said she is "changing things up a bit" next year. Little, a wife and mother of two, would like to devote more of her time to her family in 2027.

Because of this, Little said her commitments to both being a pit reporter in the Cup Series and a play-by-play announcer for NASCAR's lower-level series is too time-consuming. Little is appreciative of every opportunity FOX has given her and appreciates her time in the booth.

Here is the statement Little put out via social media:

"Starting next season, my focus will be on the NASCAR Cup Series pit road and select IndyCar races. My kids are still young and deserve more of my time."

"Thank you to everyone who has watched and supported my journey as a play-by-play voice for ARCA and the Truck Series the last six years. It's been quite a ride and one I'll always be thankful to have experienced. A special thank you to FOX for always giving me opportunities."

FOX Sports, which has broadcasted NASCAR Cup Series races since 2001, will once again be the exclusive home for the first slate of Cup Series races in 2027. The season will kick off with the Daytona 500, NASCAR's most prestigious race, which FOX has broadcasted every year since 2007.

Longtime play-by-play announcer Mike Joy, soon-to-be NASCAR Hall of Famer Kevin Harvick, and retired NASCAR driver Clint Bowyer are all expected to return to the FOX booth next year.

FOX Sports will air the first 12 Cup Series points-paying races in 2027 and wrap up its slate with the All-Star exhibition at North Wilkesboro in May.

#2709. Colts keep RB Jonathan Taylor at NFL trade deadline, reportedly turned down offers of second-round picks

The Indianapolis Colts were aggressive sellers at the trade deadline.

But the most prominent potential trade piece on their roster is staying put. Per NFL Insider Tom Pelissero, the Colts declined to trade three-time Pro Bowl running back Jonathan Taylor ahead of Tuesday's NFL trade deadline.

Per the report, Indianapolis turned down multiple offers of second-round picks to keep Taylor in a Colts uniform. The Colts would have only considered a "blockbuster" return to part with Taylor, according to the report.

It's a curious decision for a team that's given up on the season and faces what looks like a long road back to relevance.

Taylor has been one of the league's most reliable and productive backs throughout his seven-season NFL career. At 27 years old — toward the end of the traditional running-back prime — he's a potential difference-maker for a team seeking to compete for a championship now. The Colts are not that and don't project to be anytime soon.

But Taylor has been the face of the Colts through most of his career and is a fan favorite. That holds value in Indianapolis, so much that the Colts reportedly turned down multiple reasonable offers that would have provided a valuable asset to build for the future.

Amid the failures of extending Daniel Jones and trading two first-round picks for Sauce Gardner, the Colts fired longtime general manager Chris Ballard in October after a 2-4 start. This triggered a fire sale in Indianapolis that featured the trades of All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson and former Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner on the same day on Oct. 27.

Indianapolis continued its roster purge Tuesday with the trade of wide receiver Keenan Allen to the 49ers as the trade deadline approached. Hours later, the Colts reportedly agreed to trade wide receiver Josh Downs to the Chiefs.

But Taylor is reportedly staying put alongside Jones on an offense that looks little like it did when the Colts started the season with hopes of competing for the playoffs.

#2706. ‘Thank goodness he’s on our team’: Cooper Flagg makes history, Dallas Mavericks keep stacking wins

With the Dallas Mavericks down 13 points late in the first half on the second night of a back-to-back, Monday night at American Airlines Center looked very much like a schedule loss. Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving had other ideas, though, as they combined for 78 points, fueling Dallas past the Indiana Pacers in a wild finish, 125-122.

The win was the Mavericks' third straight and moved Dallas to 7-4 on the season. It also put the Mavs three games over .500 for the first time since March 1, 2025, a date that feels a lot longer ago than it actually is for anyone who has lived through the last two years of Mavericks basketball.

Think about where this franchise was not long ago. The Luka Doncic trade. Irving's torn ACL. A 26-56 season and back-to-back years without a playoff appearance. Oddsmakers set Dallas' win total at 34.5 before this season, and after an opening stretch that included Houston, San Antonio and Oklahoma City, a lot of people expected the Mavs to be scrapping just to stay afloat by mid-November.

Instead, the Mavs are stacking wins, Flagg looks like an MVP candidate in year two, and Irving looks like his old self before the ACL injury happened. Most importantly, the way the Mavs are winning these games feels sustainable. Here are some of the biggest storylines from Monday night's thriller.

DALLAS, TEXAS – NOVEMBER 9: Cooper Flagg #32 of the Dallas Mavericks dunks during the first half against the Indiana Pacers at American Airlines Center on November 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Flagg was good in the first half, but he was on an entirely different level in the second.

The 19-year-old star scored 30 of his season-high 43 points after halftime, including 14 on 6-of-6 shooting in the third quarter and 16 more in the fourth. He finished 16-of-25 from the field, 3-of-6 from 3-point range and a perfect 8-of-8 at the free-throw line, adding 10 rebounds, six assists, three steals and a block for his fourth straight double-double.

Flagg became just the second teenager in NBA history to post at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a game, joining Kevin Durant, who put up 42 points, 13 rebounds and six assists in the final game of his rookie season with Seattle in 2008. Per StatMuse, add the three steals, and Flagg is the first teenager ever with a 40-10-5-3 line.

It was also his fifth career 40-point game, as many as the next two teenagers on that list combined (LeBron James with three and Anthony Edwards with two). His 14th career 30-point game moved him into second place for the most by a player under 20, behind only James, and his seventh 35-point game tied James for the most by a teenager. And keep in mind, Flagg doesn't turn 20 until Dec. 21.

Mavericks head coach Dusty May pointed to how complete Flagg's scoring package has become.

"He gets to the rim," May said in his postgame media availability. "I think him almost being a left-handed player in the paint certainly helps. He's a great left-footed jumper, left-handed finisher. Then he's able to square in the air from 15, 17 feet. … The last couple of games, he's made some threes and he's making all of his free throws. That's how you put up the 43 points, where you do a little bit of everything."

It's almost unreal just how good Flagg already is, and May is just happy he's on his roster and not having to gameplan against him.

"He affects the game in so many ways and he makes the right plays as far as passing," May said. "Thank goodness he's on our team. It's unbelievable that he's a 19-year-old doing this."

Flagg's deadly midrange shot, which he worked on all offseason, is paying off in a big way, especially in clutch situations, where he leads the league in clutch points.

"I think just being able to get to my spots at a higher level and being more comfortable with that has allowed me to take a little bit of load off my body," Flagg said. "Just kind of stopping short, raising up over people. It's taxing going downhill all the way to the rim and trying to finish over seven-footers all night, every night. … Just trusting the work, trusting the spot work that I put in all summer long."

Through 11 games, the reigning Rookie of the Year is averaging 25.9 points, 6.9 rebounds, 6.9 assists and 2.2 steals per game. Again, given everything Mavs fans have been through over the last 21 months, this sort of euphoric rise back to genuine happiness watching these games is hard to believe.

DALLAS, TEXAS – NOVEMBER 9: Kyrie Irving #11 of the Dallas Mavericks celebrates after scoring a three point basket during the second half against the Indiana Pacers at American Airlines Center on November 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Flagg was the closer on Monday night, but Irving was arguably the reason Dallas was still in the game in those closing moments.

Playing the second night of a back-to-back for the first time this season, a day after logging 28 minutes in a 130-93 win over Brooklyn, Irving poured in 35 points in a season-high 38 minutes. He knocked down a season-high seven 3-pointers on 10 attempts, went 3-of-3 at the line and finished a game-best plus-29.

After missing 19 months with the torn ACL he suffered in March 2025, Irving said he told his teammates in the locker room after Sunday's win that he planned to play.

"When you're in a combative sport such as basketball, some days are going to feel good, some days aren't, especially coming off an injury or a long period of time," Irving said. "So I just had to get my body back used to being in the flow of the game. … I was just feeling great, and just coming in to today."

May, who said plus-minus is often overblown in a one-game sample, made an exception for Irving in this one.

"His plus-29 tonight was very indicative of how important he is," May said. "When we were struggling to make shots in the first half, we thought we were generating really good looks. We just looked a little bit flat. I thought Kyrie's shot-making just kind of righted the ship for us."

It's still early, but seeing Irving look this healthy and proving to be a seamless fit next to Flagg bodes well for what this team can accomplish this year. Perhaps the last two years of the basketball injury gods punishing the Mavs will result in some good injury luck the rest of this season.

DALLAS, TEXAS – NOVEMBER 9: Cooper Flagg #32 of the Dallas Mavericks celebrates with teammate Kyrie Irving #11 of the Dallas Mavericks after scoring a basket during the second half against the Indiana Pacers at American Airlines Center on November 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The most encouraging part of all of this is just how naturally Flagg and Irving shared the scoring load against Indiana. The two combined for 26 fourth-quarter points, including Dallas' first 13 of the period, and May said neither player blinks when the play call goes to the other.

"We're coming out of a timeout, we may draw up a play for one of them just because the other one might have an All-League defender on him, or whatever the case, and they never roll their eyes," May said. "They know when we're going to one of the two, the other one's very, very supportive because they have that much respect for each other."

Irving, an established champion who has shared the floor with more than a few superstars over his 15-year career, is grateful that he's able to be Flagg's teammate, despite the two players being on different ends of their careers.

"We keep calling him a teenager, but he plays way beyond his years. We've got to give him his flowers," Irving said. "Most young guys will probably move away from that contact, but it seems like this newer generation that's coming into our league, they fear nothing. And I think he falls right in line with that. So grateful to have him on the wing with me."

Those feelings are mutual for Flagg: "Just having [Kyrie] out there, his gravity opening the floor for everybody else, it makes my life so much easier."

DALLAS, TEXAS – NOVEMBER 9: P.J. Washington #25 of the Dallas Mavericks celebrates a three point basket during the second half against the Indiana Pacers at American Airlines Center on November 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images

It wasn't pretty at the end, but it didn't have to be for the Mavs to come up with another win. That's one thing that's been so encouraging about this fast start to the season. Dallas is finding different ways to win, whether it's pretty or not.

Indiana's Pascal Siakam torched Dallas for 26 first-half points on 8-of-9 shooting, but the Mavs adjusted their help defense after the break and held him to just three points on 1-of-7 shooting the rest of the way. The Pacers took a 66-56 lead into halftime and a 93-90 lead into the fourth before Flagg buried a 26-foot pull-up 3 to tie it. Irving's 23-footer with 9:36 left put Dallas in front for good.

Leading 125-122 with a chance to put the game on ice, PJ Washington missed a pair of free throws with four seconds left, and Caleb Martin bailed everyone out by stealing Andrew Nembhard's inbounds pass to Siakam with 0.9 seconds remaining. Pacers head coach Rick Carlisle was adamant that Martin fouled Siakam on that final play, but judging from the replays, it looked like Martin got all ball before ever making any contact with Siakam.

It obviously would've been nice for Washington to sink at least one of those free throws to avoid that last-second drama, but again, the Mavs keep finding different ways to win. How many times over the past two years have we seen a game like that end in a loss for Dallas?

DALLAS, TEXAS – NOVEMBER 9: Cooper Flagg #32 of the Dallas Mavericks goes to the basket during the first half against the Indiana Pacers at American Airlines Center on November 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images

As good (and fun) as the Mavs have been early on, Irving knows his team still has a long way to go to get to the level they want to be at.

"We haven't earned anything in this league yet," Irving said. "We consistently do it every night, and that's how you build your identity in this league and you earn your respect. We try not to put the cart before the horse."

With that being said, though, Mavs fans have earned the right to enjoy this start and, dare I say, dream big again. After two years of nothing but gut punches, a 7-4 start built on a generational teenager, a healthy veteran star and a team that genuinely seems to like playing together is a foundation Mavs fans have been waiting on.

Irving acknowledged the preseason doubt, saying the team heard "a lot of the noise" and chose not to let outside voices into the locker room. If he keeps playing like prime Kyrie, though, and if Flagg keeps rewriting the record books at this current pace, those voices of doubt are going to continue to get a whole lot quieter.

The Mavericks will now hit the road for a big three-game trip that will show just how real this start is, beginning Thursday against the Minnesota Timberwolves at Target Center at 7 p.m. CT. Dallas then visits the Cleveland Cavaliers on Nov. 14 and the Boston Celtics on Nov. 15.

#2704. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2703. Lanning: Stewart incident 'didn't match our standard'

EUGENE — After Oregon wide receiver Evan Stewart was booked in Springfield Municipal Jail early Sunday morning on DUII charges, Ducks coach Dan Lanning addressed the situation at his weekly press conference Monday.

"There was an incident this weekend that didn't match our standard here in our program," Lanning said. "There will be an appropriate action taken. Still gathering some details with what that situation looks like. But that would be handled internally. I'm not gonna respond to any other questions about that. We're gonna handle that with our guys.

"There's an expectation of what you have to... how you have to act, and how you need to perform in our program. Kind of overshadows the success that we had on Saturday, which is disappointing, but that will be handled by us internally. I'm not going to speak on it publicly."

When Lanning was asked a follow-up question about a rumored speeding incident involving other Oregon football players, for which there haven't been any confirmed arrests, he said, "I was talking about the same thing when I first addressed it."

This is also the second instance of an Oregon football team member facing DUII charges in the past year. In April, running backs coach Ra'Shaad Samples allegedly backed his Ford F-150 into a parked car outside a bar in Eugene. His next court date is Oct. 27.

An arraignment for Stewart in his DUII case hasn't been set, as official charges haven't been filed to Springfield Municipal Court as of Monday evening, according to court records.

Stewart leads the Ducks this season with 27 catches for 352 yards and four touchdowns. He missed Saturday's win over Nebraska due to an undisclosed injury.

Oregon (4-2, 2-1 Big Ten) is preparing for a road game at Illinois (3-3, 1-2) at 12 p.m. PT this coming Saturday.

#2700. Grading the trade: Josh Downs gives Chiefs WR help they needed, but is he the right fit?

Just prior to the trade deadline, the Kansas City Chiefs acquired wide receiver Josh Downs from the Indianapolis Colts. The Chiefs will receive Downs and a 2027 seventh-round pick, and the Colts will get back fourth- and fifth-round picks in 2027.

Downs, 25, who recently requested a trade, got his wish and now will team up with Patrick Mahomes. In nine games (seven starts) with the Colts this season, Downs caught 33 passes for 354 yards and one TD on 57 targets.

Downs also had a team-high seven catches for 72 yards on nine targets in the Colts' 33-30 loss in Kansas City back in Week 2.

Who won this trade? Let's dive into the debate.

The Chiefs were in big need of adding receiver help. Not one wideout on the roster has either 50 targets or 300 yards receiving on the season. Downs, sharing the lead role in Indy along with Keenan Allen (and with Alec Pierce hurt), has surpassed both marks.

That's not to say that he instantly will become Patrick Mahomes' go-to target. But it's hard not to imagine Downs stepping in and earning a fairly sizable role in Kansas City's offense, assuming he can develop a relationship with Mahomes and pick up the playbook quickly.

Downs has primarily been a slot receiver in his career, although his work rate playing outside has increased slightly in 2026 out of need. It would make sense to put him in the slot, although what makes him, Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy attractive is that they can line up in multiple spots.

Rice's numbers over the past year-plus have been slightly better inside, but Worthy has been far more efficient as a perimeter receiver in his career. That likely means Downs can take those snaps and do what he does best: run efficient routes, separate quickly and generate first downs. The biggest drawback is that Downs is not a deep threat, which was probably their biggest need.

This move also can help the Chiefs' punt-return situation. Nikko Remigio has struggled in that role this season. Downs has only returned two punts this season, but he has a very respectable 9.8-yard career average on punt returns.

The Chiefs know that Downs is a free agent after the season, and they had to be comfortable with the idea of this trade potentially being a half-season rental. Thinning out their Day 3 pick allotment stings a little, but the price wasn't that steep in the big picture, especially when you compare it to what the Seahawks paid for Rashid Shaheed (fourth- and fifth-round picks) and what the Jaguars dealt for Jakobi Meyers (fourth- and sixth-rounders) before last year's deadline.

This move is about taking advantage of a championship window with Mahomes showing he's recovered from his knee injury and Travis Kelce still performing at a relatively high level in his expected swan-song season.

Downs requested a trade and got his wish. The Colts likely weren't convinced they had to extend him, and Downs probably wasn't returning to Indianapolis next season anyway, so trading him now made perfect sense instead of waiting for compensatory-pick returns more than a year from now.

It fits right in line with the other trades they've made since firing GM Chris Ballard, shipping out one-time franchise pillars Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner and also dealing Allen. When you consider what they got back for Downs, which was two early Day 3 picks, it was a pretty fair market price.

Not having a first-rounder next spring from the Sauce Gardner will continue to sting. But with the trades, they've managed to replenish the cupboard a bit. They already have seven Day 3 picks to work with and are projected to receive two more compensatory selections in that same range.

Having those picks can allow the Colts potentially to slide up in the draft, and quarterback could be on the menu given the uncertainty surrounding Daniel Jones, even if Jones was not traded by the deadline.

They'll also eventually need to replenish a gutted WR room, but for now the Colts can see what they have in the likes of Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, Anthony Gould, Ashton Dulin, Deion Burks, Laquon Treadwell and, of course, Pierce, when he's back healthy again. It wouldn't be stunning if the Colts only bring back a few of these players next year, but the remainder of the season will help them decide who stays and who goes.

#2699. Views from the Game: Rockets defeat Nuggets 110-100; TDS speaks with Kevin Durant, Alperen Sengun

The Houston Rockets faced the Denver Nuggets in unfamiliar territory on Monday. The Rockets entered Monday night's game on their first two-game losing streak of the season after their 102-99 loss to the Phoenix Suns on Saturday.

In that game, the Rockets struggled from the field as the Suns led by double digits in the first quarter. The Rockets eventually got back in the game and even took a six-point lead at one point in the second half. Still, even a fourth-quarter resurgence from Alperen Sengun, who struggled the first three quarters, wasn't enough to keep the Rockets from dropping their second straight game.

The Rockets welcomed the Nuggets, who are coming off a win down in Mexico City over the Los Angeles Clippers. The Rockets have been without Steven Adams and Clint Capela for several games and also added Oscar Tshiebwe to their injury report with an illness. That means the Rockets will be without all three of their backup centers, leaving Sengun as the only active center for Monday's game.

Ime Udoka did mention how both Steven Adams and Clint Capela are targeting the upcoming road trip, specifically the Washington and Miami games, as possible return dates. That would be a welcome sight for a Rockets team that currently ranks 12th in rebounding after being near or at the top every season of Ime Udoka's Rockets tenure.

The Rockets got off to a fast start, led by Durant, who made his first three shots, including one from beyond the arc. Durant was as aggressive in the first quarter as he has been in several games. The quarter was back and forth, as neither team could get much separation.

The Nuggets started to take advantage of the Rockets' lack of depth at center as Jokic went to work once Sengun went to the bench. However, the Rockets put together a good finish to the quarter, and a Tari Eason 3-pointer put them up 32-24 at the end of the first quarter. Durant led all scorers with 11 points in the first 12 minutes.

The Rockets carried that momentum into the second quarter, scoring the first 11 points and building a lead of as much as 19. The Rockets played with much more force and composure than in their first half against the Suns. The Rockets had 13 assists out of their first 20 made baskets. The Rockets maintained the lead, taking a 54-40 lead into halftime.

The third quarter saw the Nuggets cut the lead to under double digits early as they started the quarter on fire from the field. The Rockets, meanwhile, saw their shooting fall off a cliff, starting 2-for-14 from the field as the Nuggets came back from an early 18-point deficit to tie the game at 5:02.

That's when Marcus Smart and Tari Eason entered the game, and the Rockets' defensive intensity immediately rose. The Rockets strung together good defensive possessions that led to easy baskets and pushed the lead back to nine at 71-62. Despite a rough start to the quarter, the Rockets led 77-68 heading into the fourth quarter.

In the fourth quarter, both teams played at a high level for the first time. On one end, Sengun scored in the paint; on the other, Jamal Murray could not miss from mid-range. The Rockets had a slim six-point lead midway through the fourth quarter.

That's when Sengun took over: he not only scored in the paint to give the Rockets a 98-90 lead, but he also assisted on the next two baskets, helping the Rockets put the game away with a 110-100 win. The win snapped the Rockets' first two-game losing streak of the season.

After the game, Ime Udoka, Kevin Durant, and Alperen Sengun spoke to the media. Udoka said the Rockets did a much better job taking care of the basketball and distributing it, and that they finished with 29 assists. SB Nation asked Durant whether it is easier to figure out the defense when he's initiating the offense.

Sengun helped close out the Nuggets with his own great passing and running the pick-and-roll with Durant. Here are both players praising each other's games after last night's win.

The Rockets now begin preparing for their old nemesis, Steph Curry and the Golden State Warriors, who come to town Wednesday with an 8-3 record and have won their last eight games.

#2698. Cardinals place QB Gardner Minshew and WR Michael Wilson on IR

The Cardinals placed quarterback Gardner Minshew and wide receiver Michael Wilson on injured reserve Tuesday, the team announced.

Minshew tore the UCL in his elbow and will miss the rest of the season. Wilson’s neck injury will end his season.

“Not the ending I had envisioned, but grateful for the journey,” Wilson wrote on social media. “Regardless of what happens, my love for the game will never change! Thank you for all the love and support. The story is still being written.”

Wilson played eight games in 2026, making 51 receptions for 546 yards and two touchdowns.

In two appearances, Minshew completed 38 of 53 passes for 354 yards and three touchdowns, and led the Cardinals to an overtime win in Dallas in Week 8. He is scheduled to be a free agent at the end of the season.

The Cardinals signed veteran quarterback Josh Johnson and rookie quarterback Joey Aguilar to back up rookie Carson Beck. Beck will get his first NFL start on Sunday against the Rams.

Aguilar was on the Jaguars’ practice squad, and Johnson was on the Bengals’ practice squad.

The Cardinals also signed receiver Phillip Dorsett II to the practice squad and released tight end Rivaldo Fairweather and running back Jermar Jefferson from the practice squad.

#2696. Who will call plays for Oregon after Mehringer's firing?

EUGENE — After firing first-year offensive coordinator Drew Mehringer seven games into the 2026 season, Dan Lanning shared Oregon's plans for filling his role moving forward at his weekly press conference Monday night.

Offensive assistant Jay Johnson will lead offensive playcalling for the Ducks going forward, Lanning said.

"He has a lot of experience as a play-caller, was with me in Georgia when we were part of the national championship team," Lanning said. "Went on to have a lot of success in Colorado and Michigan State. He's gonna lead the efforts there with the offensive staff, but it'll still be a collaborative effort, with a lot of the work that we do.

"He's also coming in with a different perspective, a different view, not being with us the last few years, where he can provide a couple things that might be different than what we've done."

Mehringer, previously the tight ends coach for the Ducks, is the first assistant coach Lanning has fired in his tenure at Oregon, which began in 2022. The Ducks' offensive decision-making was at the center of intense criticism over the past three weeks, during which Oregon averaged just 14 points per game and lost twice to UCLA and Illinois.

Lanning spoke to the human element of letting Mehringer go.

"They see the football coach, right? That's also an unbelievable dad. A great husband," Lanning said. "The guy's been part of our staff for the last five years, that's done some really good things here, and I think all of us feel like we shoulder some of the blame. Because we didn't create success for our team this season."

#2695. What We Learned from the Spurs win over the Suns

It's hard not to feel like you're watching a mirage during some of these games. The level of play is excellent and the bits and pieces you might be tempted to pick at are scarce. The wins are piling up. The vibes are good. Everything is going according to plan. Nothing to see here…right?

Right! Look, I'm not going to even try to play devil's advocate here. No one wants to be the guy pointing at the Alien dropping 40 and 11 over 25 minutes and saying, "actually, this is bad." If that's a take you'd like to read then I can assure the internet is full of people willing to take you up on the offer. For my part, and if you've come to this website today, I'm assuring you, I genuinely find it hard to think of a less interesting angle to come at this from.

Victor Wembanyama is simply brilliant. He's been brilliant, he's brilliant now, and he only seems to be getting more brillianter as we go along. Twelve of his fifteen made shots on Monday were dunks or layups, and nine of those were dunks. Four different teammates threw him an alley-oop. The Spurs are running a dizzying array of different motions that all end up at the same destination, which is a Wembanyama dunk. The threes, instead of feeling like something he has to do to open up the lane, now just arrive in the natural rhythm of the game. He made two threes all night, a digestif tacked on at the end of a satisfying meal.

Vic even hit a Dream Shake in the middle of the 2nd quarter that left me staring off in the distance in disbelief.

I sometimes try to avoid writing about the Victor Wembanyama of it all when I do these because it feels too easy. What did we learn from the Spurs win? They still have the best player on the planet and he helps a lot. Case closed. To his credit, he goes out of his way to make ignoring him next to impossible.

The problem, if there is one, is that regular season basketball does actually seem easy for him at this point. That's not a mirage. I have no doubt about how hard he's worked to achieve the level he's currently operating on, but that doesn't change the fact that watching him dismantle the average NBA team every other night doesn't look very challenging. He's like Will Hunting ranting at Professor Lambeau about how easy it is to solve those supposedly impossible graph theory equations.

Victor's ascension this season is impressive, and I want to do my best to appreciate the casual brilliance we are privy to on a regular basis, but that greatness comes at a cost, and that cost is a raised ceiling. I simply don't care that he can drop 50 on the Mavs or 40 on the Suns. I don't care that he can snuff out the Blazers. I'm sure there will be another jaw-dropping stat line on Wednesday when he plays the Bulls, and I'm sure it will be met with another polite nod from me.

None of this is his fault, mind you. The schedule is the schedule and the teams are the teams. He's taking care of business, and that's all you can really ask of him.

I guess I've just spent the last nine games of this winning streak telling myself I still don't know what I'm looking at and I really believe anyone who tells you they do is lying. The ease with which they are winning these games is real. Every conclusion we draw from it…well, that's a little more hazy. I try to grab on to things I know. "The Spurs are Good." "The Suns are Bad." "Wemby is Tall," and project out from there but I end up feeling like I'm chasing the ghost of a conclusion. The idea of a resolution instead of an actual one.

This is a champagne problem at most. Like, what, I'm having a bad time because I can't tell if the Spurs are great, really great, or generationally amazing? A few years ago we were sitting through a sixteen-game losing streak and then an eighteen-game one, on our way to the lottery again and again. Now I'm hemming and hawing because our first brush with success last spring has got me feeling antsy.

The thing I'm dancing around here is that the Finals loss is an albatross around our necks that we're just going to have to wear. There's no two ways about it. I'm encouraged by the things I'm seeing from this new three-guard- Hydra, but I won't feel comfortable until I know it can outscore Jalen Brunson when he's going Nuclear. I love that Victor seems more calm and assured in his decision making, but I still have nightmares about KAT finding a way to neutralize him. Every time we race out to a lead this season, my brain remembers the blown leads in June.

The context of the past clouds everything from the present and I don't think there's an easy fix for that feeling. It shouldn't sully our enjoyment of the current moment, but it does ground the results in a certain reality.

All of this is certainly real enough, but none of it really matters.

I don't feel qualified to talk about what Dylan Harper is doing. It's a level of basketball that I recognize as great but have difficulty quantifying, because my analysis tends to err on the side of "oh my God, how did he do that?" Nuance exits the room when he has the ball in his hands. There is a grace and fluidity to his game that is hypnotic, whether he's getting to the basket with relative ease or casually spinning into a midrange jumper. I don't know how to say this as a compliment, but it's fascinatingly boring to watch. He's operating at breakneck speed but still in complete control, sort of like how F1 cars can look a little blah during a race until you blink and realize they're going like 200 mph.

The caveat with Dylan is, obviously, his youth. It's simultaneously the most exciting and frustrating thing about him. That control I just alluded to can prove elusive sometimes. Sometimes he seems almost like he's just watching the game happen to him and forgets that he's more than capable of grabbing the reins. He started the game last night a little bit adrift. Whether that's a byproduct of the three-guard lineup's growing pains or him simply sitting back and watching Wemby cook like the rest of us, he was kind of invisible, and a guy like Harper just shouldn't be invisible. After the game, Mitch talked about calling him out specifically during a timeout in the 3rd, and that wake-up call seemed to snap him back into place. He absolutely torched the Suns in that 3rd quarter, going 6-of-8 from the field and effectively putting the game out of reach after Phoenix briefly tried to make a run. He is, without a doubt, the 2nd best player on the team from a talent perspective, and that this already kinda feels indisputable is the most shocking thing of all.

It would've been so easy to just write off De'Aaron Fox this season, as evidenced by that fact that so many people did, in fact, write him off. But he's been really fun to watch so far this year. I love the way he fits into the similar but different skill sets of our guards, and he seems a little more freed up now that Harper and Castle can take on more responsibility. He's still so fast and he still has great vision, and last night he finished with 15 points, six assists and nine rebounds. His chemistry with Wembanyama has only gotten better, with four of those six assists going to Wemby, and their propensity for lobs and oops of all types seems to have rubbed off on everyone around them. It's kind of exactly what you would want from a veteran leader in the starting lineup. Everyone else is right though, the Spurs probably should've just shipped him last summer because everyone on Twitter was mad.

Are you ever going to stop having an existential crisis about the Spurs this season?

Are you kidding? My entire brand is "existential crisis about the Spurs." What would I even write about if not that?

You could analyze the gameplay? Trending stats? Maybe break down different plays the offense runs? Talk about defensive schemes?

You sound insane right now. Completely bonkers.

I just think people come here trying to figure out what they learned from the game and you're only even talking about the journey through the dark night of the soul you went through on a random Monday. We're eleven games into the season! You don't want to, like, build to that?

Shooters shoot. I'm not going to lie to the readers about the fact that I can't sit still and watch Wembanyama dunk on dudes without stressing about the inexorable march of time or whatever.

I'm not asking you to lie, but also, like, can you not sit still and just watch Wembanyama dunk on dudes without stressing about the inexorable march of time or whatever? Like, are you incapable of doing that?

#2693. Cardinals place QB Gardner Minshew and WR Michael Wilson on IR

The Cardinals placed quarterback Gardner Minshew and wide receiver Michael Wilson on injured reserve Tuesday, the team announced.

Minshew tore the UCL in his elbow and will miss the rest of the season. Wilson's neck injury will end his season.

"Not the ending I had envisioned, but grateful for the journey," Wilson wrote on social media. "Regardless of what happens, my love for the game will never change! Thank you for all the love and support. The story is still being written."

Wilson played eight games in 2026, making 51 receptions for 546 yards and two touchdowns.

In two appearances, Minshew completed 38 of 53 passes for 354 yards and three touchdowns, and led the Cardinals to an overtime win in Dallas in Week 8. He is scheduled to be a free agent at the end of the season.

The Cardinals signed veteran quarterback Josh Johnson and rookie quarterback Joey Aguilar to back up rookie Carson Beck. Beck will get his first NFL start on Sunday against the Rams.

Aguilar was on the Jaguars' practice squad, and Johnson was on the Bengals' practice squad.

The Cardinals also signed receiver Phillip Dorsett II to the practice squad and released tight end Rivaldo Fairweather and running back Jermar Jefferson from the practice squad.

#2692. Damian Lillard is back and Ja Morant is here. How exactly is this going to work? | Bill Oram

In the history of basketball, we have certainly seen some why-would-they-do-that? pairings.

Jerseys and sleeves. Kawhi Leonard and a tree sponsorship. Utah and "the Jazz."

Once, there was even Detlef Schrempf and a headband, if you can believe that.

We're about to find out if they belong on such a list.

Because of all the things you might have said the Trail Blazers needed as they prepared to welcome Lillard back after making a playoff run without him, a slight-of-stature ball-dominant guard with a questionable jump shot would not have topped anyone's list.

Depth on the wing? Yes. Shooting? Definitely. Defense? Always.

Morant doesn't particularly address any of those, and yet, he's here, a dynamic two-time All-Star in need of a second act, being paid a team-high $42.1 million to play the same position as not just Lillard, but Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson.

Heck, the Blazers' most valuable point guard last season was forward Deni Avdija.

"I'm sure there will be questions about fit," General Manager Joe Cronin said Monday.

The Blazers have little more than three weeks before the regular season begins in which to figure that out. At the team's annual media day on Monday, Morant appeared in a fresh white No. 1 Trail Blazers jersey. It's happening.

"It's easy for people to be like, 'Man how is this going to work,'" Lillard offered. "'They can't do this, they can't do that.' But being on the floor with them … we can be a dangerous team and I really believe that."

The onus is on the Trail Blazers starting this month to prove that they bet right in acquiring Morant. And that pairing him with Lillard isn't the boondoggle conventional wisdom suggests it will be.

Lillard noted how many teams that succeeded in the playoffs last year, think San Antonio with its four point guards, relied on numerous playmakers. To his credit, Morant said he would be comfortable coming off the bench, if necessary.

But they would not be the first NBA team to fall into the trap of believing they are capable of adjusting or that they will be comfortable sacrificing. It isn't uncommon to see players in those situations default to familiar habits and sensibilities once the season is underway or struggles come.

That's what made a lot of the positive energy around what sure seems like an awkward roster ring so hollow. We're going to need to see it to believe it.

Morant tried to lay out a vision for how it could look. If he drives to the paint and is double-teamed, someone else is inevitably open. That's how basketball works.

"That allows me to have more space to be the best Ja I can be," Morant said.

The 36-year-old Holiday, who would be a more natural complement next to Lillard or Morant than they are to each other, made his own case for why the point guard rotation makes sense.

"It's about being a complete basketball player for myself," he said, "and I think we have a lot of guys like that."

There is a long history of teams talking themselves into superstar additions that make little sense. The Los Angeles Lakers once made a conscious decision to acquire Russell Westbrook and pair him with LeBron James. Nobody made them do that!

The talent and star power of a Lillard-Morant backcourt is undeniable. Still, I remain unconvinced that Cronin, with a very hands-on new owner in his ear, made the deal with winning basketball games at the front of mind.

Although, admittedly, Cronin's biggest wins as a GM have been in the trade market.

The haul of assets he collected for Lillard, only to get him back two years later, will go down as an all-time great swindle. So, too, will the oft-questioned Avdija trade a year later.

Maybe he sees something in a Lillard-Morant pairing that many of us can't.

Morant could return to the All-Star form he had achieved before injuries and off-court issues derailed his ascent. And if he does, the Blazers can either trade him for pieces that fit better or clear out the logjam and build around him.

But to sell the current roster as a basketball strategy doesn't quite pass the smell test.

Neither Lillard nor Morant has achieved stardom due to his defensive acumen. Each player needs the ball in his hands to thrive. If the duo is on the floor together, Avdija is no longer the secondary playmaker, he becomes tertiary.

So, you are left to wonder whether the Blazers sold themselves on Morant because of how he can help the current collection of talent or if they simply saw the opportunity to land a 27-year-old All-NBA talent for cheap, regardless of what it meant for the existing roster construction.

And if you're being honest, you probably don't need to wonder which of the two it is.

"We were very focused and we'll continue to be on … adding to our talent base as much as we can," Cronin said.

That thinking right there may tell you just how far ahead of everyone else the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder are in the Western Conference. They are positioned to dominate for the next half-decade, if not longer. The only chance any other team has of disrupting that is taking bold risks.

But I thought the goal was to go all in on the twilight years of Lillard's career?

"Dame literally just wants to win," said first-year head coach Micah Nori, whose charge is to sort out arguably the most talented glut of point guard talent in NBA history. "I think that's the only thing left he really has to (do). He's already proven he's a winner, but at the highest level."

Does adding Morant move Lillard closer to a title? Or simply give Portland a potential off-ramp if Lillard is no longer the same player after tearing his Achilles tendon?

Morant was without question a low-risk, high-reward addition. He came at the reasonable price of Jerami Grant and Kris Murray. If it becomes clear that Morant is one point guard too many, or that he's just not the player he once was, some will argue that it didn't cost the Blazers much to try.

However, there is an opportunity cost to messing with Lillard's swan song. If you don't get it right, you risk wasting the gift of his voluntary return last summer. And, not for nothing, Lillard has the option to become a free agent again after this season.

The franchise icon certainly hasn't said anything that would suggest he is unhappy about Morant's presence, although he stopped short on Monday of a full-throated endorsement. He said he knew about the trade before it went through.

When I asked if he thought it was a good idea right away or if he needed time to get on board with the plan, Lillard said, "My position on it was, I'm prepared for whatever."

It's good that he's already thinking about other positions. Because his old one is getting awfully crowded.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Philadelphia opened the season with a 7-0 loss to the rival Pittsburgh Penguins, and coach Rick Tocchet described his team's play as "disturbing." There was only one way for the season to go after that, right? Wrong.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Tocchet's bunch entered the season with a lot of well-earned optimism. Even with subpar play from Matvei Michkov last season, the Flyers managed to reach the Eastern Conference Semifinals. Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#2688. Fernando Mendoza gets 3-word message from Kirk Cousins after Raiders trade

Fernandomania has officially begun in the desert.

With the Las Vegas Raiders trading quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings in before Tuesday's NFL trade deadline, Las Vegas are expected to turn to Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 pick in the draft earlier this year, under center.

Mendoza is slated to make his first career start against the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks at home on Sunday, Nov. 15 (4:05 ET).

Mendoza's lone regular-season action came during his debut, at the end of a Week 4 road loss to the New England Patriots on Oct. 11. He finished 6-for-8 passing for 48 yards.

Mendoza's first two opponents boast vaunted defensive units. Seattle's defense, dubbed the "Dark Side" for a reason, did not allow a touchdown last week to the undermanned Arizona Cardinals. Looking ahead, the Raiders face the Denver Broncos on the road in Week 11. Denver ranks in the top 10 in points allowed per game (20.7), sacks (26) and takeaways (12).

"I feel that Fernando has done a great job," Cousins told reporters Oct. 26. "He has a bright future ahead. I'm going to try and go out there and play as well as I possibly can and try and win and give him a good example to learn from."

On his Instagram story, Cousins offered a goodbye to "Raider Nation" and a message to Mendoza, whom Cousins tagged in the post.

Toughening matters for Mendoza on the field will be the lack of a rushing attack for the Raiders. First-round talent Ashton Jeanty from the 2025 draft has not worked out, although rookie Mike Washington has shown some juice in the backfield. Still, Las Vegas ranks 31st in rushing yards per game (71.3) and is last in yards per rush (2.9).

Similar to Cousins, Mendoza will likely have to shoulder much of the output in the Raiders' offense.

"The game has to be balanced," head coach Klint Kubiak said following the team's most recent loss to the San Francisco 49ers that dropped their record to 4-5. "You can't be a running and throwing team when you're throwing it every time. That's not easy.

"You got to start the game a lot faster. You got to go toe-to-toe in the first half so that the second half isn't a throwing fest."

The good news is that tight end Brock Bowers ranks ninth in the league in receiving yards and provides a crucial red-zone target with six touchdowns already this season. Wide receiver Tre Tucker emerged as a reliable downfield option for Cousins, which gives Mendoza more relief in the passing game.
